topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Mental multiplication and division (age 9+)
topic.description: Multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts, including related facts and place-value adjustments
evidence: Calculate 40 × 60 mentally by using 4 × 6 = 24 then appending zeros
Derive 7 × 15 by calculating 7 × 10 + 7 × 5
Calculate 360 ÷ 9 mentally using 36 ÷ 9 = 4
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out things like '24 × 5' or '360 ÷ 8' in their head — using clever connections to known facts rather than needing to write anything down?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply and divide mentally drawing on known facts, related facts and place-value adjustments (40×60 via 4×6; 7×15 via 7×10+7×5; 360÷9 via 36÷9).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 3.OA.7/3.OA.5 (strategies) and 5.NBT.1–2 (place-value scaling) applied to mental calculation.
• Operational details — this extends Y4 mental strategy to LARGER numbers via three moves: (1) scale a known fact by place value (40×60 = (4×6)×100 = 2400; 360÷9 = (36÷9)×10 = 40); (2) partition and use the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5 = 105); (3) derive from a near/related fact. The recurring danger with (1) is the 'append zeros' shortcut applied without place-value understanding — keep it grounded as scaling. Encourage flexible CHOICE of strategy and comparing methods; the aim is efficiency and flexibility, not one prescribed route.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): scale a known fact (30×40 via 3×4). Tier B (age 9–10): use partitioning for 7×15 and place-value scaling for 360÷9. Tier C (age 10): choose and justify the most efficient mental strategy for a mixed set and explain the place-value scaling.
bestPractices: Scale known facts by place value (4×6 → 40×60) understood as ×100, not 'append zeros', so it survives decimals.
Teach partitioning via the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5) with an area-model backing.
Use the ×÷ inverse and related facts to derive division mentally (360÷9 from 36÷9).
Foster flexible strategy CHOICE — compare methods for the same calculation and discuss which is most efficient.
Verbalise the chosen strategy and check reasonableness against an estimate.
keyRepresentations: Known-fact-scaled-by-place-value chains (4×6 → 40×60 = 2400)
Area/partition model for distributive mental multiplication (7×15)
Place-value chart — the scaling behind ×÷ by tens/hundreds
Number line / derived-fact links for division
commonMisconceptions: 'Appending zeros' without place-value understanding, misfiring on decimals or miscounting zeros (40×60 as 240 or 24000).
Partitioning incorrectly (7×15 = 7×10 + 5, dropping the second multiplication).
Not using the inverse/related facts for division, computing from scratch.
Fixating on one strategy rather than choosing the most efficient.
Losing a place value in ÷ scaling (360÷9 as 4 rather than 40).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, mentally multiply and divide larger numbers by drawing on known facts, related facts and place-value adjustments: scale a known fact by place value (40×60 = (4×6)×100 = 2400; 360÷9 = (36÷9)×10 = 40), partition using the distributive law (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5 = 105), and derive from related facts. The goal is flexible, efficient strategy CHOICE and reasoning about place value — not a single prescribed route, and not a 'just append zeros' trick.

activities.title: Scaling studio: watch the known fact grow
feedback: If a learner gives 240 for 40×60: ask 'what is a ten times a ten?' Guide to 4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400 — both numbers contributed a ten, so two zeros.
If a learner gives 24000: have them recount — only one hundred factor arises from tens×tens, so the known fact 24 is scaled by 100, giving 2400 (24000 would be scaling by 1000).
If a learner gives 360÷9 = 4: prompt 'you found 36÷9 = 4; 360 is ten times 36, so the answer is ten times bigger — 40.'
If the digit-sliding helps, confirm: 'the digits moved two places left; each place to the left is worth ten times more, so two places is ×10×10 = ×100.'
activities.rationale: Grounding ×÷ by tens/hundreds as place-value scaling of a known fact keeps the method correct for decimals and helps guard against miscounted zeros, a common misconception at this stage.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts.
Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
Mental strategies build on properties (3.OA.5) and fluency (3.OA.7) with place-value scaling (5.NBT.1–2).
learnerActions: Take 40×60 and name the known fact hiding inside it (4×6=24).
Place 24 on a place-value chart and scale it by ×100, watching the digits slide two columns to the left to make 2400 — because a ten times a ten makes a hundred, and both numbers contributed a ten.
Explain in units: '4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400', so the answer has two zeros, not one.
Try the same scaling move on a division: link 360÷9 to the known fact 36÷9=4, then scale by ×10 to get 40.
Contrast with a tricky case where a naive 'add a zero' rule would mislead (e.g. a decimal such as 0.4×60, which is 24, not 240) to feel why scaling by place value is the reliable idea.
Optionally use a live place-value chart where the digits visibly shift columns, rather than zeros simply appearing, to make the scaling felt.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying/dividing by tens and hundreds scales a known fact by place value; tens×tens makes hundreds, so the number of zeros follows from the place-value reasoning, not from a memorised 'append a zero' rule.

activities.title: Partition to make it friendly
feedback: If a learner writes 7×15 = 7×10 + 5 = 75: point to the area model — the second tile is 7×5, not 5. Both parts must be multiplied by 7.
If a learner stalls trying to recall 7×15 whole: prompt 'split 15 into 10 and 5 — which of those are easy to multiply by 7?'
If both tiles are computed but added wrong, have them re-add 70 + 35 and compare to the estimate.
activities.rationale: Partitioning via the distributive law with an area-model backing gives a reliable derived-fact route and directly corrects the common error of dropping the second multiplication.
sourceClaims: Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
Y5 pupils multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts.
learnerActions: Take 7×15 and split 15 into friendly parts: 10 and 5.
Compute 7×10 = 70 and 7×5 = 35, then add: 70 + 35 = 105. State both multiplications explicitly so the second part is not dropped.
Back the partition with an area model: a rectangle 7 wide split into a 7×10 tile and a 7×5 tile, whose areas sum to the whole.
Say the full reasoning aloud and check it against an estimate (7×15 is a little over 100).
activities.intendedInsight: The distributive law lets you break a hard factor into friendly parts and multiply each part, then recombine — so you only need facts you already know.

activities.title: Two routes, same answer: choosing the friendliest
feedback: If both routes give different answers, help locate the slip by re-stating the known fact in each route.
If a learner always uses the same method, ask them to find a second route and compare effort — reinforce that either is correct and efficiency can depend on the numbers.
Praise explicit justification of a choice ('I used scaling because 36÷9 is a fact I know').
activities.rationale: Comparing methods for the same calculation builds flexibility and efficiency, the stated aim of mental calculation at this level.
sourceClaims: Scaling known facts by place value and distributive partitioning are efficient mental strategies; teach flexible strategy choice, not 'append zeros'.
learnerActions: Take 7×15 and solve it two different ways: (a) partition into 7×10 + 7×5, and (b) factor-scaling (15 = 3×5, so 7×15 = (7×5)×3 = 35×3, or 7×3×5 = 21×5).
Confirm both routes land on 105.
Discuss which route felt quicker for this calculation and why.
Repeat the compare-methods habit on a mixed set and justify the most efficient choice for each item.
Optionally present the same calculation in more than one worked form side by side so the alternatives can be compared directly.
activities.intendedInsight: Mental maths is about selecting the friendliest of several valid routes to the same answer, not following one prescribed procedure.

activities.title: Explain-aloud diagnostic and quick checks
feedback: Full response: mentally combines a known fact with correct place-value or partitioning adjustments across × and ÷, explaining the reasoning.
Partial: derives some facts (e.g. 7×15) but mishandles place-value scaling in 40×60, or needs prompting for the division link — revisit the scaling studio.
Gap: appends wrong zero-counts, has no derived-fact strategy, or defaults to a written algorithm — return to known facts and the scaling/partition models.
If the method is right but a single arithmetic slip occurs, do not reteach: have the learner re-state the known fact and re-apply the adjustment; this often lets them self-correct on recheck.
activities.rationale: Listening to the spoken strategy (especially on 40×60) is intended to help distinguish genuine place-value understanding from a memorised zero-count; the quick checks are recognition/fill-in/spot-the-error items, so they consolidate and verify a chosen method but do not by themselves elicit independent strategy construction. Efficacy is not established by this rewrite.
learnerActions: Do 40×60, 7×15 and 360÷9 in your head while explaining your reasoning aloud for each.
Answer a few quick checks to consolidate: choose the quickest way to do 7×15 among options; complete 40×60 = (4×6)×□; find the error in a worked solution where zeros were miscounted.
For each check, re-state the known fact at the core and the place-value or partitioning adjustment you applied.

Answer and justify the probe prompts: how many zeros does 40×60 have and why two not one? how did you break up 15? what small division fact hides inside 360? if you know 4×6=24, what else can you work out quickly?
activities.intendedInsight: A correct mental method pairs a known-fact core with a correct place-value or partitioning adjustment, and you can verify your answer by explaining and estimating.

constraints: Keep ×÷ by tens/hundreds grounded as place-value scaling of a known fact, not 'append zeros' — the latter can lead to miscounted zeros (e.g. when the known fact already ends in zero, as in 50×40 = 2000) and fails on decimals.
When partitioning, require BOTH parts to be multiplied (7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5), not 7×10 + 5.

Recognition/fill-in-the-blank and spot-the-error checks consolidate and verify a chosen strategy but do not by themselves elicit independent strategy construction; pair them with explain-aloud production.
Tap-to-reveal strategy cards anchor the methods but let the learner see rather than try alternatives; use them as a reference scaffold, not as the main practice.
A coaching dialogue ('what known fact helps? is there a quicker route?') can rehearse strategy selection but will not on its own build mental speed or show the place-value scaling visually.
Live-updating place-value charts, draggable area tiles and side-by-side worked routes are optional interaction examples to make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.

errorPatterns.nextMove: reason in units: 4 tens × 6 tens = 24 hundreds = 2400; count that BOTH numbers contributed a ten, so two zeros. Avoid the bare 'add a zero' phrasing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer has too few zeros; child says 'four sixes are 24, add a zero'

errorPatterns.pattern: cannot partition for 7×15 — has no derived-fact route, tries to recall it whole or gives up
errorPatterns.nextMove: model 7×15 = 7×10 + 7×5; rehearse partitioning the harder factor into friendly parts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child stalls on 7×15 rather than splitting 15 into 10 and 5

errorPatterns.pattern: does not use the inverse/place-value link for 360÷9 — does not see 36÷9 inside it
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt 'what's 36 ÷ 9? so what's 360 ÷ 9?' — bind the larger division to the known small fact and the place-value shift.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child attempts long division or is stuck rather than using 36÷9 = 4 then scaling

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Written Multiplication & Division
topic.description: Write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods
evidence: Calculate 23 × 4 using partitioning (20 × 4 + 3 × 4)
Calculate 96 ÷ 8 using known table facts
Begin to use a formal written layout for short multiplication
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '23 × 4' or '68 ÷ 4' — either in their head using times table knowledge, or by writing it out step by step?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y3, US Grade 3–4). Writing and calculating ×÷ statements using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, moving from mental methods toward formal written methods.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y3 'write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using the multiplication tables that they know, including for two-digit numbers times one-digit numbers, using mental and progressing to formal written methods'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.NBT.3 'multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10'; building toward 4.NBT.5 'multiply … using strategies based on place value … illustrate and explain using … area models'.
• Operational details: the engine is PARTITIONING via the distributive law — 13×4 = (10×4) + (3×4) — made visible with the AREA MODEL / grid method, which is the conceptual bridge to the formal column algorithm. Start mental (partition, known facts) and progress to a recorded grid before the compact written form.
• Checkpoint: partition and calculate. Tier A (7): multiply a teen by a single digit by partitioning (13×4 = 10×4 + 3×4). Tier B (7–8): use a grid/area model to calculate a 2-digit × 1-digit product. Tier C (8): explain how the grid's partial products correspond to the distributive law and combine them correctly.
bestPractices: Anchor two-digit × one-digit in PARTITIONING and the distributive law: split the tens and ones, multiply each, recombine (13×4 = 10×4 + 3×4 = 40+12 = 52).
Use the area model / grid method as the visual of the distributive law — the array grown up — so the formal method later has meaning rather than being a rote procedure.
Progress deliberately from mental partitioning → recorded grid → compact written form, keeping the link between them explicit so children can fall back to meaning.
Use known table facts as the building blocks (10×4 and 3×4 must be secure) and connect × with ÷ (write the matching division statement).
Emphasise place value throughout — the '10' in 13 contributes 10×4=40, not 1×4 — to pre-empt the classic column-multiplication place-value error.
keyRepresentations: Area model / grid method (distributive law made visible)
Partitioning into tens and ones
Arrays scaled up to the area model
Expanded then compact written layout
commonMisconceptions: Place-value error: treating the tens digit as ones (13×4 done as 1×4 + 3×4).
Forgetting to combine ALL partial products (computing 10×4 and 3×4 but not adding them).
Multiplying digit-by-digit without regard to their place value.
Not connecting the grid/area model to the numbers (seeing it as a separate trick).
Losing the link between the mental partition and the written record, so the written method becomes meaningless steps.

learn.summary: For children aged 7–8 (UK Year 3, US Grade 3–4) learning to write and calculate two-digit × one-digit multiplication (and matching division) by partitioning via the distributive law. The core engine is splitting a number into tens and ones, multiplying each part, and recombining — e.g. 13×4 = (10×4)+(3×4) = 40+12 = 52. The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible as the bridge from mental partitioning to the formal written method. Guidance progresses deliberately: mental partitioning → recorded grid → expanded then compact written layout, keeping the link explicit so the written method carries meaning rather than being memorised as steps.

activities.title: Splitting a rectangle: area model for 13×4
feedback: If a learner multiplies only one piece (e.g. gives 80 for 23×4 and forgets 3×4), point back to the uncounted region of the rectangle: 'This 3×4 part is still inside the rectangle — count it and add it in.'

If a learner treats 20×4 as 8 (multiplying the bare digit 2 and dropping the zero), keep the place-value name attached: '2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80', and show the tens region is 20 columns wide, not 2, so its area is ten times the 2×4 = 8 they computed.

If both partial products are correct but the sum slips (e.g. 80 + 12 = 82 instead of 92), do not reteach the method — ask them to re-add carefully and estimate (23×4 is about 100, so 82 looks too small).

Confirm success when a learner partitions by place value, multiplies every part with its correct place value, recombines accurately, can point from each partial product in the expanded form back to the matching grid region, and can explain how the carried ten in the compact form comes from the ones region.
activities.rationale: Anchoring two-digit × one-digit in partitioning and the distributive law, with the area/grid model as its visual, gives the later formal method meaning and pre-empts the classic place-value error of treating the tens digit as ones.
sourceClaims: Y3: write and calculate statements for × and ÷ using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods.
The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible and is the conceptual bridge from partitioning to the formal column algorithm.
learnerActions: Draw or view a rectangle 13 units wide and 4 units tall and cut it with a vertical line at the boundary between the tens and the ones, so it becomes a 10×4 piece and a 3×4 piece.
Work out the product for each piece (10×4 = 40 and 3×4 = 12) and write the number inside each region.
Add the two partial products to find the whole area: 40 + 12 = 52.

Line the grid up next to the expanded written form (40 + 12), saying which partial product matches which region of the grid. Then look at the compact column layout and explain how the 12 from 3×4 becomes 2 ones and a carried ten, which joins the 4 tens from 10×4 to make the 5 tens in 52.
Repeat with 23×4: split into 20×4 = 80 and 3×4 = 12, then combine to 92.
activities.intendedInsight: A two-digit × one-digit product is the sum of the partial products from each place-value part; the '10' in 13 contributes 10×4 = 40 (not 1×4), because you must multiply the whole value of the tens, not just its digit.

activities.title: Moving the split line — the distributive law felt as area
feedback: If a learner thinks a different split gives a different answer, have them recompute both partial products and add again; the totals agree because the whole rectangle is unchanged.
If a learner splits 13 as '1 and 3' rather than '10 and 3', recolour or relabel the tens region to show it is 10 wide, not 1 wide — the area 10×4 = 40 makes the error visible.
Praise reasoning that connects the chosen split to easy known facts, not just a correct number.
activities.rationale: Letting the split point vary while the total holds steady makes the distributive law a felt, general property rather than a one-off trick, and reinforces why place-value partitioning is the convenient choice.
sourceClaims: The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible and is the conceptual bridge from partitioning to the formal column algorithm.
learnerActions: Starting from a 13×4 rectangle already split at the tens/ones boundary, split the same rectangle (its width of 13) at a different point — for example into a 9×4 piece and a 4×4 piece (note 9 + 4 = 13, so the total width is unchanged) — and compute the two new partial products (36 and 16).
Check that whatever point you split at, the two partial products still add to the same total (52).
Discuss why the split at the tens/ones boundary is the most useful one: it uses known facts (10×4 and 3×4) and lines up with how the number is written.
State the rule in words: splitting the rectangle into parts and adding the parts' areas always gives the whole area.
activities.intendedInsight: The product is unchanged by how you partition — the distributive law — and partitioning by place value is chosen because it lands on known facts and matches the written numerals.

activities.title: Linking multiplication to division with known facts
feedback: If a learner has no strategy for 96÷8 and resorts to slow counting, prompt 'what times 8 is near 96?' and offer the partition 96 = 80 + 16.
If a learner divides only one part, point out the remaining part still needs dividing, just as with multiplication.
Confirm success when the learner reaches the division fluently via known facts and checks it by multiplying back or estimating.
activities.rationale: Connecting × with ÷ and binding division to secure known multiplication facts strengthens both and uses the same partitioning engine, preventing division from being treated as an unrelated procedure.
sourceClaims: Y3: write and calculate statements for × and ÷ using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods.
learnerActions: Write the division that matches a multiplication fact you have made (e.g. from 10×4 = 40 write 40÷4 = 10).
Solve 96 ÷ 8 by partitioning: split 96 into 80 + 16, divide each by 8 (80÷8 = 10, 16÷8 = 2) and recombine to get 12.
Alternatively, ask 'what times 8 is near 96?' and use the known fact 8×12 = 96.
Check the answer by multiplying back: 8×12 = 80 + 16 = 96.
activities.intendedInsight: Division can be reached through known multiplication facts and the same place-value partitioning, so multiplication and division are two views of the same relationship.

activities.title: Grid-to-written-method reference and check
feedback: If a learner picks the trap answer 16, return to the grid: the tens region is 10×4 = 40, so the answer cannot be as small as 16.
If a learner computes both partial products but cannot locate them in the written layout, line the grid beside the expanded form and match region to numeral together.
Treat this as a companion consolidation once the model is understood, not a first encounter with the idea.
activities.rationale: A labelled area-model diagram and matching exercises consolidate the correspondence between grid and written method and test the classic place-value pitfall directly; this is reference and consolidation rather than the first interactive build of the concept.
sourceClaims: The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible and is the conceptual bridge from partitioning to the formal column algorithm.
learnerActions: Given a completed grid, fill in each partial product and then the total, then write the same calculation in the expanded form (e.g. 40 + 12) and the compact column form.
Match a grid diagram to the written calculation that goes with it.
Tackle a check question with the common trap answer present — for 13×4, explain why 16 is wrong (it comes from 1×4 + 3×4, treating the tens digit as ones) and why 52 is right.
Point to each region of a grid and say where its partial product appears in the expanded written method, and how it contributes (including any carry) to the compact form.
activities.intendedInsight: Each step of the written method corresponds to a region of the grid; spotting the place-value trap answer shows understanding of why the tens must be multiplied as tens.

constraints: Known table facts are prerequisites: 10×4 and 3×4 (and similar) must be secure before combining them, and division work relies on known multiplication facts — reteach the relevant facts if they are shaky.

Progress in order — mental partitioning, then recorded grid, then expanded, then compact written form — keeping the link between stages explicit so children can fall back to meaning rather than memorising disconnected steps.
Keep place-value names attached throughout ('2 tens × 4 = 8 tens = 80') to pre-empt the error of multiplying bare digits.

A fixed, labelled diagram can show and teach the correspondence between grid and written method; being able to move the split line and watch partial products recompute is an added affordance for building the distributive insight interactively, not a claim that a static image cannot teach this.

Matching and fill-in checks can confirm whether the method and its pitfalls are grasped, but do not by themselves require the learner to construct the full method from scratch; pair them with building and explaining activities.

An area model is planar; use squared paper, cut-out rectangles, or a screen grid as convenient — none is uniquely necessary, and a paper cutout (which has slight real thickness) approximates the idealised flat area model well enough that this does not affect the mathematics.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 13×4 = 52 via 10×4=40 and 3×4=12 (checks out); 23×4 = 92 via 20×4=80 and 3×4=12 (checks out — the assessment's stated answer 92 and partial products 80 and 12 are correct); 96÷8 = 12 via 80÷8=10 and 16÷8=2, confirmed by 8×12 = 80+16 = 96; the alternate split 9×4=36 and 4×4=16 also sums to 52. No erroneous alternative (e.g. '60' or '82') is presented to learners as valid; these appear only as error patterns to watch for and correct.

The source describes the variable-split activity as a 'killer moment' of dragging a split line; this is retained as an interactive affordance example, not a required mechanism, and the same insight can be reached on paper by comparing different splits.

Source claims for CCSS-M (3.NBT.3 / 4.NBT.5) and the NCETM bridging claim are marked verified:false in the original and should be treated as unconfirmed; the DfE Y3 claim is marked verified:true in the legacy data but has not been re-checked here.

probeDeeper: You split 23 into 20 and 3. Did you multiply BOTH pieces by 4? Show me each.
Why is 20 × 4 equal to 80 and not 8?
For 96 ÷ 8, which times-table fact helped you?
Estimate 23 × 4 roughly — is your answer close to that?
assess.correctAnswer: 23 × 4 = 92 (20×4 = 80, 3×4 = 12, 80 + 12 = 92). 96 ÷ 8 = 12 (e.g. 80÷8 = 10 and 16÷8 = 2, or knows 8×12 = 96). The teacher watches for partitioning by place value, multiplying every part, and recombining — not just multiplying the tens digit.

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies only one part — does 20 × 4 = 80 and forgets 3 × 4, giving 80; or multiplies the digits as if 2 and 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: use an area model / grid: a 23-by-4 rectangle split into a 20-by-4 and a 3-by-4 region; both regions must be counted and added.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 80 (dropped ones) or 8×4-style digit multiplication ignoring place value

errorPatterns.pattern: partitions the tens wrongly — treats 20×4 as 8 (multiplies the digit 2, forgets the zero) so 8 + 12 = 20

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; multiply 2- and 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number using formal written (short) multiplication, including carrying, and check with estimation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'multiply two-digit and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout' (short multiplication), building on Y3 mental→written 2-digit×1-digit.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.5 — 'Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number … using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations; illustrate and explain … using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.' (CCSS emphasises area/place-value strategies before the compact algorithm.)
• Operational details — the formal algorithm must be built ON the area/partitioning model, not taught as disconnected digit-manipulation. Progression: partition (47×6 = 40×6 + 7×6), lay out as an area model / grid method, then compress to the columnar short-multiplication layout where carrying records the regrouped tens/hundreds. Insist children can explain what the 'carried' digit means (it's regrouped place value). Estimation first (47×6 ≈ 50×6 = 300) frames a reasonable answer and catches place-value errors.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): 2-digit × 1-digit with the grid/area method (43×3). Tier B (age 8–9): 3-digit × 1-digit short multiplication with carrying (234×5) and an estimate. Tier C (age 9): explain each carried digit as regrouped place value and connect the compact layout back to the area model.
bestPractices: Build the algorithm from the area/grid method: 47×6 as 40×6 + 7×6 laid out as two sub-rectangles, THEN compress to the columnar form so 'carrying' is understood as regrouping, not a rule.
Require an estimate before calculating (rounding a factor) to set an expected magnitude and catch place-value slips.
Make the meaning of the carried digit explicit — it is regrouped tens/hundreds, written and then added in — not a mysterious little number.
Use place-value counters/columns alongside the written digits during the transition so each written step maps to a concrete regrouping.
Practise with numbers that force carrying in different columns, and check answers against the estimate and via the inverse.
keyRepresentations: Area/grid model (partition each factor by place value) — the conceptual home of short multiplication
Place-value columns with counters — makes carrying = regrouping visible
The compact columnar layout with the carry digit recorded
Estimation on a number line / rounding — to bound the answer
commonMisconceptions: Treating carrying as a meaningless ritual and misplacing or forgetting the carried digit.
Multiplying only the ones and 'adding' the tens digit rather than multiplying it (place-value error): 47×6 giving 42+... wrong.
Aligning digits incorrectly or dropping a place, producing answers off by a factor of 10.
Not connecting the compact method to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.
Skipping estimation, so a wildly wrong magnitude goes unnoticed.

learn.summary: For ages 8–9, build formal short (columnar) multiplication of 2- and 3-digit numbers by a 1-digit number ON TOP of the area/grid model so that 'carrying' is understood as regrouping place value, not a ritual. Core examples: 47×6=282 and 234×5=1170.

activities.title: Method bridge: area model beside the columns
feedback: If the tens digit comes out far too large, check whether you added the carry before multiplying: multiply the digit first (5×3=15), THEN add the carried number (+2=17).
If the answer is off by a factor of ten, check column alignment — only one digit belongs in each column and the extra ten/hundred must travel one place left.
When the area sub-products (1000+150+20) sum to exactly the column answer (1170), you have connected the two methods correctly.
If a single-digit product is wrong (e.g. 5×4 recorded as 25 instead of 20), pause and shore up that specific table fact before continuing.
activities.rationale: The UK Y4 standard requires using the formal written (short multiplication) layout; US 4.NBT.5 and NCETM guidance place that procedure on place-value and area/array strategies, and estimating first helps catch place-value slips. Showing the area model and columns updating together is a proposed way to make 'carry = regroup' concrete and self-checkable; it has not been separately validated here.

learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding a factor, e.g. for 234×5 use ≈200×5=1000 (or ≈50×6=300 for 47×6), and write the estimate down before calculating.
Draw an area/grid model splitting a factor by place value: for 234×5 make three sub-rectangles 200×5, 30×5 and 4×5; for 47×6 make 40×6 and 7×6.
Set out the same calculation in a short-multiplication column layout right next to the area model.

Work each partial product in the columns in lockstep with the matching sub-rectangle. For 234×5: 5×4=20 → write 0 in the ones and regroup 2 tens; 5×3=15, +2=17 → write 7 in the tens, regroup 1 hundred; 5×2=10, +1=11 → write 1 in the hundreds and 1 in the thousands, giving 1170.
Say aloud what each carried digit means, e.g. 'the little 2 is 2 regrouped tens'.
Add the area sub-products (1000+150+20=1170) and check they equal the columnar answer exactly.
Compare the finished answer against your estimate; if it is off by a factor of ten, look for a misaligned column.
activities.intendedInsight: The carried digits are the area model regrouped and folded into columns — multiply the digit first, THEN add the carry, keeping one digit per column.

activities.title: Make the carry visible with place-value counters
feedback: If you wrote a two-digit partial product all in one column, remember each column holds only one digit — the extra ten must move left as a counter.
If you forgot to carry, check whether any counters are left stranded in a column that should hold at most nine.
activities.rationale: Place-value counters alongside the written digits let each written step map to a concrete regrouping, a proposed way to target the 'carrying is a meaningless ritual' misconception.
sourceClaims: The formal written algorithm should be built from the area/grid model and place-value regrouping, with estimation used to check magnitude.
learnerActions: Under the column headings, lay out the first factor with place-value counters as many times as the one-digit multiplier says (e.g. 6 groups of 47 for 47×6), so the counters show the whole product.
As you compute each partial product, physically move a regrouped ten (or hundred) one column to the left to represent the carried digit.
Match each counter move to the little digit you write above the next column.
Narrate: 'ten ones regroup into one ten, so the ten moves left.'
activities.intendedInsight: Carrying is the physical act of regrouping ten of one unit into one of the next place; the written carry records that move.

activities.title: Annotated worked example as a reference anchor
feedback: Use this as a model to copy the layout and language, then work a fresh calculation yourself — a worked example shows the structure but does not test whether you can carry correctly on your own.
activities.rationale: A static annotated worked example is a strong reference anchor for the area-to-column link; its limit is that it does not give feedback on a learner's own fresh calculation.
sourceClaims: The formal written algorithm should be built from the area/grid model and place-value regrouping, with estimation used to check magnitude.
learnerActions: Study a worked 234×5 with the area model above and the matching short-multiplication below.

For each column, read (or reveal) the explanation of the partial product and what its carry stands for, e.g. 'this is 2 regrouped tens' (from 5×4=20) and 'this is 1 regrouped hundred' (from 5×3=15, +2=17).
Match each area sub-rectangle to the column it feeds into.
activities.intendedInsight: Every column in the compact method has a home in the area model, and every carry names a specific regrouped place value.

activities.title: Consolidation and error-spotting checks
feedback: Correct for 47×6: 6×7=42, write 2 carry 4; 6×4=24, +4=28, so 282. The carry is added AFTER multiplying.
For 234×5 the estimate ≈200×5=1000 tells you 1170 is reasonable; an answer like 117 or 11700 signals a misaligned column off by a factor of ten.
These items consolidate and assess the procedure; pair them with the area-model work so errors can be self-diagnosed, not just marked wrong.
activities.rationale: Short multiplication is procedurally checkable, so targeted fill-in, estimate-choice and spot-the-error items can consolidate it; the limit is that they test the procedure rather than building the area-model link, so they complement rather than replace it. No original source claim directly supports this consolidation principle.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing carry digit in a partly-worked 47×6.
Choose the best estimate for 234×5 from given options and justify the rounding.
Spot the error in a worked calculation where a carry was forgotten, and correct it.
Spot the error where someone added the carry before multiplying (e.g. did (4+4)×6=48 for 47×6) and explain the fix.
activities.intendedInsight: Short multiplication fails in specific, visible ways — a wrong magnitude, a missing carry, or a carry added before multiplying — and these can be diagnosed and corrected.

Multiply the digit first, THEN add the carried number; do not add the carry before multiplying.
Only one digit per column; the regrouped ten/hundred travels one place left.
The written method assumes automatic recall of the relevant table facts; if single-digit products are slow or wrong, shore those up separately.

Worked examples and annotated references anchor the structure but do not give feedback on the learner's own fresh calculation.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply up to 4-digit × 1-digit AND 2-digit × 2-digit using formal long multiplication, illustrated with the area model.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.5 — 'fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm'; 4.NBT.5 covers up to 4-digit × 1-digit with area/place-value strategies.
• Operational details — the new challenge over Y4 short multiplication is the TWO-DIGIT multiplier: 34×27 requires multiplying by both the ones (7) and the tens (20), then adding partial products. The area model (45×23 as four sub-rectangles 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3) is the conceptual scaffold that shows WHY there are two rows of partial products and why the second row is shifted (it's ×20, not ×2). The classic error — forgetting the placeholder zero on the second partial product — is precisely a lost-place-value error the area model prevents. Estimate first (34×27≈30×30=900) to bound the answer.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): 4-digit × 1-digit (2347×6) securely. Tier B (age 9–10): 2-digit × 2-digit long multiplication (34×27) with correct partial-product placement. Tier C (age 10): draw the matching area model and explain why the second partial product is shifted / carries a zero.
bestPractices: Anchor long multiplication in the area model: 2-digit×2-digit as four sub-rectangles, so the two partial-product rows and the shift are seen as ×ones and ×tens.
Make the placeholder zero meaningful — the second row is ×20 (tens), not ×2 — rather than a rule to 'put a zero down'.
Estimate first by rounding both factors to bound the answer and catch magnitude errors.
Progress grid method → expanded partial products → compact long multiplication, keeping the area link visible.
Check with the inverse or by comparing to the estimate; watch carrying across multiple columns.
keyRepresentations: Area/grid model with four sub-rectangles (the home of the partial products)
Expanded partial-products layout bridging grid to compact form
Compact long-multiplication layout with the placeholder zero
Estimation (rounding both factors) to bound the product
commonMisconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the second partial product (treating ×20 as ×2).
Multiplying only by the ones digit of the two-digit multiplier and forgetting the tens.
Carrying errors across several columns, or adding carries into the wrong place.
Misaligning partial products when adding them.
Not connecting the algorithm to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning formal long multiplication (up to 4-digit × 1-digit and 2-digit × 2-digit), anchor the written algorithm in the area model so the two partial-product rows and the placeholder zero become meaningful place-value facts rather than memorised rules. The central objective: the child sees that the second partial-product row is '×20 (tens)', not '×2', and that the four sub-rectangles of an area model sum to the same total as the two added partial products. Estimation by rounding both factors bounds the answer and catches magnitude slips.

activities.title: Bridge the area model to the written method (34 × 27)
feedback: If the second partial product comes out as 68 instead of 680: you multiplied by 2 instead of 20. Look at the 34×20 region of your grid — it is twenty rows worth 680, not 68. Write the zero first to reserve the ones place, saying 'we are multiplying by twenty'.

If you only computed 34 × 7 and stopped: every part of 27 (both the 20 and the 7) must multiply every part of 34. Check your grid has all four regions — a missing region means a missing partial product.
If you wrote 34×2 + 34×7: you split 27 into digits 2 and 7 without place value. The tens digit is worth 20, so draw the ×20 regions explicitly.
If 238 + 680 doesn't total 918, recheck your column alignment and any carries — your estimate of ~900 tells you the answer should be near there.
activities.rationale: Coupling a partitioned area model to the columnar layout makes the place value of each partial product (and the meaning of the placeholder zero) visible, so a lost place value can be self-diagnosed. A live split-screen where partitioning tiles fill the long-multiplication frame, with tiles sliding together to show 600+210+80+28 = 918 matching the two added partials, is one concrete way to make this mechanism visible; a running estimate panel can flag magnitude slips.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding both factors: 34 × 27 ≈ 30 × 30 = 900, and keep this estimate in view as you work.
Draw an area model for 34 × 27 and partition it into four labelled sub-rectangles: 30×20, 30×7, 4×20, 4×7.
Alongside, set up the long-multiplication layout and compute the first partial product 34 × 7 = 238 (which is the 30×7 and 4×7 tiles: 210 + 28).
Compute the second partial product 34 × 20 = 680, writing a 0 in the ones place FIRST because this whole row is ×20, i.e. tens (this is the 30×20 and 4×20 tiles: 600 + 80).
Add the two partial products: 238 + 680 = 918, and confirm it matches the sum of all four area tiles (600 + 210 + 80 + 28 = 918).
Check the result against your estimate of 900 — are they close?
activities.intendedInsight: The second partial-product row is shifted and carries a placeholder zero because it is ×20 (tens), not ×2; the four area sub-rectangles are exactly the same quantities as the two written partial products broken apart, so the algorithm and the area model are two views of the same calculation.

activities.title: Secure 4-digit × 1-digit short multiplication (2,347 × 6)
feedback: If a carry is added into the wrong column, recheck each step and compare with your estimate. Note that rounding 2,347 DOWN (to 2,000 or 2,300) gives an underestimate, so the true answer should sit a little above those figures — 14,082 (just over 13,800) is reasonable.
If any column is skipped, remember every digit of 2,347 must be multiplied by 6.
activities.rationale: This activity enacts the Y5 curriculum requirement to multiply a number up to four digits by a one-digit number using a formal written method; it also secures the carrying and place-value fluency that two-digit long multiplication builds on, forming a sensible progression before the two-row layout.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers.
learnerActions: Estimate first: 2,347 × 6 ≈ 2,000 × 6 = 12,000 (or 2,300 × 6 = 13,800 for a tighter bound).
Compute 2,347 × 6 in formal written layout, carrying across each column: 7×6=42 (write 2 carry 4), 4×6=24 plus 4 = 28 (write 8 carry 2), 3×6=18 plus 2 = 20 (write 0 carry 2), 2×6=12 plus 2 = 14.
Read off the answer 14,082 and check it against your estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a multi-digit number by a single digit requires multiplying every digit and correctly handling carries across several columns; estimation bounds the magnitude.

activities.title: Map each written partial product to its area region (45 × 23)
feedback: If a region is missing or a partial product doesn't account for the full value of a digit, redraw the grid so every part of 23 (20 and 3) multiplies every part of 45 (40 and 5).
If the ×20 partial product lacks its placeholder zero, link it to the 800 + 100 = 900 tens regions: the row lives in the tens.
If the two totals (region sum and partial-product sum) disagree, recheck each region's arithmetic against the matching partial.
activities.rationale: Explicitly connecting the four area regions to the two partial products is the discriminating task that separates understanding from rote execution, and it directly targets the common error of omitting partial products.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Draw an area model for 45 × 23 with four regions: 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3.
Add all four regions to get the product: 800 + 120 + 100 + 15 = 1,035.
Now compute 45 × 23 by long multiplication and point to which area regions make up each partial product: 45×3 = 135 (= 120 + 15) and 45×20 = 900 (= 800 + 100).
Confirm the two partial products 135 + 900 = 1,035 equal the sum of the four area regions.
activities.intendedInsight: Each written partial product is a sum of two area sub-rectangles, so a child who can map regions to partials understands WHY there are two rows rather than following steps by rote.

activities.title: Consolidation: spot-the-error and estimate checks
feedback: For the spot-the-error item: the second row is ×20, so it must occupy the tens — the 0 marks the empty ones place, meaning '×20 not ×2'.
For the estimate item: rounding 48 to 50 and 52 to 50 gives 2,500, close to the true product 2,496, so it is a good magnitude check.
activities.rationale: Procedural consolidation with error-spotting and estimation tests and reinforces the procedure efficiently. This recognition/fill-in format checks the procedure rather than independently eliciting construction of the area link, so it is best used after the construction activities, not in place of them.
learnerActions: Examine a worked 34 × 27 in which the placeholder zero is missing from the second partial product; identify the error and explain why the zero belongs there.
Fill in a missing second partial product in a given long-multiplication layout.
Choose or state the best estimate for 48 × 52 by rounding both factors (≈ 50 × 50 = 2,500).
activities.intendedInsight: The missing placeholder zero and estimation are the quickest self-checks for magnitude; recognising the error reinforces the place-value reasoning behind the shifted row.

constraints: Recognition and fill-in/spot-the-error tasks consolidate the procedure but do not elicit the child independently constructing an area model and mapping it to the written method; use them after, not instead of, the bridging construction work.

Annotated static worked examples (area model above, written method below, tap to reveal each partial product's region) are useful reference scaffolds, but a fixed example cannot give feedback on a child's own fresh calculation or their own placeholder-zero error — pair them with tasks the child computes.

Spoken dialogue alone lacks a shared visible written layout, so it cannot display aligned columns or reliably catch column-placement errors in this spatial, multi-step procedure; keep a written/drawn layout at the centre rather than relying on talk alone (this is a layout-affordance limit, not a claim that dialogue can never support the procedure).

The area model is a conceptual scaffold for place value; the goal is eventual fluent compact long multiplication with the area link available for self-diagnosis, not permanent dependence on drawing grids.
Treat carrying/alignment slips as performance errors (re-estimate and recheck the flagged column) rather than reteaching the whole method.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply and divide whole numbers AND decimals by 10, 100 and 1000, understanding the digit shift.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply and divide whole numbers and those involving decimals by 10, 100 and 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.2 — 'explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and … in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10'; 5.NBT.1 place-value ten-times relationship.
• Operational details — the essential understanding is that ×/÷ by a power of ten SHIFTS every digit left/right across the place-value columns — the digits move, the decimal point stays put (or equivalently the point moves relative to the digits). This must replace the false 'add a zero / move the decimal point' rule, which breaks for decimals (3.45×100 is 345, not 3.4500). Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart where digits physically slide. ×1000 = three places left; ÷1000 = three places right, introducing tenths/hundredths/thousandths. This underpins metric conversions and powers-of-ten notation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): × and ÷ whole numbers by 10/100 with digit-shift language. Tier B (age 9–10): 3.45×100, 72÷1000 correctly, explaining the shift. Tier C (age 10): explain why 'add a zero' fails for decimals and connect to metric conversion.
bestPractices: Teach as a digit SHIFT across place-value columns (digits move left for ×, right for ÷), not 'add a zero' or 'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
Use a place-value/Gattegno chart where digits physically slide the correct number of places, with the decimal point fixed.
Introduce tenths/hundredths/thousandths through ÷10/100/1000 so the columns to the right of the point are meaningful.
Link the number of places to the power of ten (×1000 → 3 places) and later to exponent notation.
Connect to metric conversions (m↔cm↔mm, kg↔g) as an authentic application.
keyRepresentations: Place-value / Gattegno chart with sliding digits (point fixed)
Arrow/shift diagram showing 1/2/3 places for 10/100/1000
Decimal place-value columns (tenths, hundredths, thousandths)
Metric conversion tables as an application
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero' rule misapplied to decimals (3.45×100 wrongly written as 3.4500).
'Move the decimal point' causing confusion about direction or number of places.
Shifting the wrong number of places for the power of ten.
Forgetting to fill empty places with zeros as placeholders when needed (e.g. 72÷1000 = 0.072).
Thinking dividing always makes the digits smaller in value without understanding the place shift.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 by understanding that each digit SHIFTS across the place-value columns — digits move left for multiplying and right for dividing, while the decimal point stays fixed. This replaces the fragile 'add a zero' rule, which breaks for decimals (3.45×100 is 345, not 3.4500), and the memorised 'move the point' rule, which gives the same numerical result but hides why the value changes and is easily misapplied (for example where to put the point in a whole number, or forgetting placeholder zeros). The skill underpins metric conversions and powers-of-ten notation.

activities.title: Sliding digits on a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner appends zeros to a decimal (3.45×100 → 3.4500): on the chart, multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100× more, so each digit moves two columns left — the '3' becomes 3 hundreds. The point does not move; the digits do. The correct answer is 345.

If 72÷1000 comes out as 720 or 7.2: dividing makes each digit worth a thousandth as much, so the digits move exactly three columns to the RIGHT. 720 has moved them left (the wrong direction), and 7.2 has moved them only one place right instead of three.
If 72÷1000 is written as 0.72 (too few decimal places): count every column each digit crosses and drop a zero into each empty one so 72 lands correctly as 0.072.

If the place count is off by one under speed: this may be a counting slip rather than a misunderstanding. Recount the zeros in 10/100/1000, match them to the places shifted, and check whether the error comes back on similar items.
activities.rationale: The target concept is itself a digit shift across place-value columns, so watching digits slide while the point stays fixed makes the mechanism visible and exposes why the memorised 'add a zero' rule fails for decimals. Labelling the columns tenths/hundredths/thousandths gives meaning to the places opened up by division.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.2 requires explaining patterns in zeros and decimal-point placement when ×÷ by powers of ten; 5.NBT.1 the ten-times place-value relationship.
Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with labelled columns from hundreds down to thousandths (… H  T  O • t  h  th) and a fixed decimal point.
Place 3.45 in the columns, then multiply by 100: slide every digit TWO columns to the LEFT so the 3, 4 and 5 become 345. Note that nothing was appended — the digits moved.
Now test the tempting 'just add two zeros' shortcut on 3.45 and compare: it gives 3.4500, which is wrong. Discuss why the shortcut fails for decimals.
Divide 72 by 1000: slide every digit THREE columns to the RIGHT, and fill each empty column it crosses with a placeholder zero, giving 0.072 (including the leading 0).
Compute 6 × 10 by sliding one place left (giving 60), and connect the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 (×1000 → 3 places).
Optionally switch the chart to a metric mode so the same kind of shift is reread as a conversion: metres → centimetres is ×100 (two places left) and centimetres → millimetres is ×10 (one place left).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten changes what each digit is worth, so the digits shift the matching number of place-value columns; the decimal point does not move, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Reference chart with reveal-able shift arrows
feedback: If the direction is reversed: multiplying moves digits LEFT (larger value), dividing moves them RIGHT (smaller value).
If the count is wrong: match the number of places to the number of zeros in the power of ten.
activities.rationale: A static annotated chart is a clean, reusable reference that consolidates the direction-and-count rule, though it cannot itself let a learner slide digits through many cases — pair it with active manipulation for the shift intuition.
sourceClaims: Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Study a place-value chart annotated with arrows that show the shift for ×10 (one place), ×100 (two places) and ×1000 (three places), and the reverse for division.
Answer the prompt 'why isn't 3.45 × 100 = 3.4500?' and check your reasoning against a revealed explanation.
State in your own words how many places each power of ten shifts the digits and in which direction.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference links each power of ten to a fixed number of places and direction, reinforcing that the direction and count — not zero-appending — determine the result.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and fill-in consolidation
feedback: For the 3.45×100 choice: 3.4500 keeps the point fixed and tacks on zeros, leaving the value unchanged — wrong. Sliding each digit two places left gives 345.
For 72÷1000: a missing placeholder zero gives 0.72; count the crossed columns to reach 0.072.
An off-by-one place error may be a counting slip, so recount and see whether it happens again; a wrong direction signals the digit-shift idea needs revisiting.
activities.rationale: Checkable items that deliberately include the decimal trap and placeholder cases let a learner apply and test whether the shift understanding transfers; such items consolidate, check and diagnose but do not themselves provide the digit-sliding manipulation, so use them after active manipulation.
learnerActions: Complete 72 ÷ 1000 = ___ , writing all placeholder zeros.
Choose the correct value of 3.45 × 100 from options including the trap value 3.4500, and explain why the trap is wrong.
Find and fix the mistake in a worked example where a digit has been shifted the wrong number of places.
Explain, for one of your answers, how the value of each digit changed.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidation surfaces the specific decimal trap (3.4500) and the placeholder-zero requirement (0.072), confirming whether digit-shift reasoning is secure rather than a fragile trick.

activities.title: Testing the 'just add a zero' claim out loud
feedback: If the learner defends 'add a zero': ask what each digit is now worth — in 345 the 3 is 3 hundreds, so the digits moved, they were not padded.
If they are unsure how to express it: 'multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100 times more, so each slides two columns left.'
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue can draw out and challenge the misconception by prompting the learner to test it; it works best alongside a chart where the shift can be seen, since discussion alone does not let the learner manipulate the digits.
sourceClaims: Teach ×÷ by powers of ten as a place-value digit shift, not 'add a zero'/'move the point', which mislead with decimals.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists you can always 'just add a zero' to multiply by ten.
Test the claim on a whole number (6 × 10 = 60) where it seems to work, then on a decimal (3.45 × 100) where it produces 3.4500.
Argue, using place value, why the claim is unsafe and what actually happens to the digits.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why 'add a zero' works for whole numbers but fails for decimals turns a half-learned rule into reasoned understanding of the digit shift.

constraints: Teach the operation as a digit shift across place-value columns (left for ×, right for ÷), not as 'add a zero' or 'move the decimal point': 'add a zero' gives wrong answers for decimals, and 'move the decimal point', although it gives the same numerical result, hides the change in place value and is easily misapplied to whole numbers and placeholder zeros.
Always fill empty columns crossed by a shift with placeholder zeros, including leading zeros (e.g. 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072).
Introduce tenths/hundredths/thousandths through dividing by 10/100/1000 so the columns to the right of the point are meaningful before relying on them.
Link the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in the power of ten (×1000 → 3 places) and, later, to exponent notation.

Reference charts and multiple-choice / fill-in items consolidate, check and diagnose whether digit-shift reasoning transfers, but do not themselves provide the sliding manipulation; pair them with active manipulation rather than treating them as sufficient alone.

A manipulable sliding chart, a static annotated chart, a dialogue, and consolidation items each serve a different observable purpose; none is inherently sufficient alone, and no claim is established here that only one medium can teach this.

topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use the short division ('bus stop') method to work out something like '2,457 ÷ 6', and decide what to do with any remainder left over?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 1-digit using short division (with place-value/array support), and interpret remainders appropriately for the context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using the formal written method of short division and interpret remainders appropriately for the context'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.6 / 5.NBT.6 — 'find whole-number quotients … using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division; illustrate and explain using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.'
• Operational details — short division ('bus stop') processes the dividend left-to-right by place value: at each digit ask 'how many divisors fit?', record the quotient digit, and CARRY the remainder to the next place. Understanding rests on place-value partitioning (4932÷6 = 4000+900+30+2 shared) and the ×÷ inverse (checking by multiplying back). The distinctive Y5 demand is interpreting the remainder in context: round up (minibuses needed), round down (full bags), keep as a remainder, or express as a fraction/decimal — the SAME calculation yields different answers by context. Estimate first (4932÷6≈5000ö5≈1000).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): 3-digit ÷ 1-digit short division, no remainder. Tier B (age 9–10): 4-digit ÷ 1-digit with a remainder, and state it correctly. Tier C (age 10): interpret the remainder three ways for three different contexts of the same division and check via multiplication.
bestPractices: Build short division on place-value partitioning — exchange/carry the remainder to the next column — using place-value counters so 'carrying the remainder' is understood as regrouping.
Teach remainder interpretation as context-dependent: round up, round down, keep, or express as fraction/decimal — using the same calculation in different stories.
Always check the answer with the inverse (quotient×divisor + remainder = dividend) and against an estimate.
Connect to the array/area (division as finding the missing dimension) so short division isn't a rootless ritual.
Handle the 'won't go' case explicitly (a leading digit smaller than the divisor → 0 in that place and carry), a common stumbling point.
keyRepresentations: Short-division ('bus stop') layout with carried remainders
Place-value counters/columns — exchanging the remainder into the next place
Array/area with an unknown dimension — division as inverse of ×
Number line / bar model for remainder interpretation in context
commonMisconceptions: Mishandling the remainder carry — not moving it to the next place or adding it wrongly.
Interpreting the remainder wrongly for the context (rounding down when you must round up, e.g. minibuses).
Dropping a place when the digit is smaller than the divisor (not writing the 0 and carrying).
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.
Treating short division as digit-manipulation divorced from place value/sharing meaning.

learn.summary: For learners aged 9–10: divide numbers up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using the short-division ('bus stop') method, grounded in place-value exchange, and interpret the remainder according to the context (round up, round down, keep as a remainder, or express as a fraction/decimal). The central insight is that the same calculation can yield different correct answers depending on the story, and that answers should be checked by multiplying back and against an estimate.

activities.title: Share the columns: short division with place-value counters
feedback: If a learner divides each digit independently with no carry, model the exchange explicitly: the leftover from a column becomes ten counters of the next place; write the small carried digit before dividing the next place.
If the quotient has too few digits because a place was skipped, point to the column where the divisor wouldn't go and insist on writing 0 there and carrying the whole amount on.
Confirm correct work by linking each written carry digit back to the physical exchange the learner just performed.
activities.rationale: Building the algorithm on visible place-value exchange helps 'carrying the remainder' be understood as regrouping rather than an unexplained ritual, and makes the dropped-zero error addressable at its source. Dragging/exchanging counters with live quotient digits recording above is one concrete way to make the regrouping felt; a physical set of counters serves the same purpose.
sourceClaims: 4.NBT.6/5.NBT.6 require finding quotients using place value, properties and the ×÷ relationship, illustrated with arrays/area models.
Short division should be grounded in place-value exchange; remainders must be interpreted according to context (round up/down/keep/fraction).
learnerActions: Lay out 4932 as place-value counters: 4 thousands, 9 hundreds, 3 tens, 2 ones.

Share each column left to right into 6 equal groups, starting with the thousands (4 thousands won't make a group of 6, so that place gives 0 — exchange the 4 thousands for 40 hundreds and carry them on).

When a column won't share evenly, exchange each leftover counter for ten counters of the next-lower place and add them to that column (e.g. a spare hundred becomes ten tens that join the tens column).
Record the quotient digit for each place above the bus-stop layout as you go, and write the carried amount beside the next digit.
When the divisor won't go into a place at all, write 0 in the quotient for that place and carry the whole amount onward — do not skip the place.
Finish with 4932 ÷ 6 = 822 and note there is no remainder here; then repeat with a dividend that leaves a remainder.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'carried remainder' of the written short-division method is the same idea as regrouping/exchanging place-value counters: a leftover in one column is worth ten of the next place down. Every place of the dividend produces a quotient digit, including a 0 when the divisor won't go.

activities.title: One division, three answers: interpreting the remainder in context
feedback: If a learner stops at 'r5' without interpreting it, ask what the leftover represents here (5 sweets, not enough for another full bag) and tie the number to the situation.

If a learner rounds inappropriately for the context, re-read the story together: 'Can leftover children travel with no minibus?' pushes toward rounding up; 'Is a half-full bag a full bag?' pushes toward rounding down.
Acknowledge when the learner gives different, correctly justified answers for different stories about the same calculation — that is exactly the point.
activities.rationale: Treating remainder interpretation as context-dependent, using one calculation across several stories, targets the common error of reading the remainder wrongly for the situation. A live context switcher that reframes the same leftover is one way to make this vivid; spoken stories or written word problems work too.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a one-digit number using formal short division and interpret remainders appropriately for the context.
Short division should be grounded in place-value exchange; remainders must be interpreted according to context (round up/down/keep/fraction).
learnerActions: Take a single division that leaves a remainder and solve it once — for example, 125 ÷ 8 = 15 remainder 5.

Read that SAME result (15 remainder 5) inside three different stories about 125 items: 'containers that each hold 8 — how many containers are needed for 125 items?' (round the quotient UP to 16, because the 5 left over still need a container), 'full bags of 8 — how many full bags from 125 sweets?' (round DOWN to 15, with 5 left over), and 'share 125 cm of ribbon fairly among 8 groups — how much each?' (the leftover can be split, so express it as a fraction, giving 15 and 5/8 cm each).
State in words what the leftover of 5 means in each story (e.g. '5 sweets are not enough to fill another full bag').
Decide, for each story, whether the right answer rounds up, rounds down, or keeps the remainder — and justify why.
For extra practice with the round-up case, try 52 children into minibuses of 9: 52 ÷ 9 = 5 remainder 7, which rounds UP to 6 minibuses because the 7 leftover children still need transport.
activities.intendedInsight: The same calculation gives different legitimate answers depending on what the leftover represents in the situation; interpreting the remainder is a decision about the context, not a fixed rule applied to the number.

activities.title: Estimate first, check by multiplying back
feedback: For a correct method with a single-digit arithmetic slip, do not reteach the method — have the learner verify with multiplication and estimation and locate the wrong digit (e.g. a quotient of 812 gives 812 × 6 = 4872, not 4932, which flags an error).
If an estimate is far from the result, prompt the learner to recheck which place values were shared and whether the estimate itself was rounded sensibly.
Reinforce the inverse relationship by writing the check equation alongside the division each time.
activities.rationale: Routine estimation and inverse checking address the misconception that short division is digit-manipulation divorced from meaning, and stop arithmetic slips from persisting unnoticed. A check panel that multiplies the quotient back is one convenient support; doing the multiplication by hand achieves the same check.
sourceClaims: 4.NBT.6/5.NBT.6 require finding quotients using place value, properties and the ×÷ relationship, illustrated with arrays/area models.
learnerActions: Before dividing, make a rough estimate by rounding to friendly numbers (round 4932 to about 4800, then 4800 ÷ 6 = 800), so expect a quotient near 800 — about three figures. Avoid rounding the divisor down (e.g. 6 to 5), which would inflate the estimate.
Carry out the short division to get a quotient and any remainder.
Check with the inverse: compute quotient × divisor (+ remainder) and confirm it equals the dividend, e.g. 822 × 6 = 4932.
Compare the answer with the estimate and ask whether it is sensible; if the check fails, find and fix the slip rather than re-learning the method.
activities.intendedInsight: Division and multiplication are inverses: quotient × divisor (+ remainder) = dividend. An estimate and an inverse check catch arithmetic slips and keep the quotient's size reasonable.

activities.title: Talk it through: does the leftover change the answer?
feedback: If the learner cannot justify the choice, ask a sharpening question: 'What happens to the children who don't fit on the full minibuses?'

• Age/Topic — 10–11y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 2-digit using formal SHORT division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to context; and CHOOSE short vs long division.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using … short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to the context'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.2 fluent multi-digit division; 5.NBT.6 division by 2-digit divisors — method choice is a UK curriculum emphasis.
• Operational details — the distinctive skill is METHOD SELECTION: short division by a 2-digit divisor is efficient when the divisor is 'friendly' (e.g. 16, or a divisor whose multiples the child knows/can derive quickly, 3648÷16), doing the multiply-subtract mentally at each place; long division is safer when the divisor is awkward and mental multiples are hard. Estimate first and check by multiplying back.

Carry over flexible remainder interpretation (decimal/fraction in measurement, round by context).

activities.title: Method-chooser: the same division, two ways
feedback: 3648÷16 = 228 exactly; if your answer isn't near your estimate of ~225, recheck a step.
If a short-division step went wrong, check whether your mental multiple of the divisor was correct (e.g. 16×3=48) — insecure multiples are a common cause of carry errors.

Once the quotient has started, if the divisor doesn't fit into the current part, write a zero in that place of the quotient and carry any amount on; otherwise the quotient will have the wrong number of digits (4080÷17 = 240 is a good example — the zero in the ones place matters because 17 does not go into the final 0).
If you found short division error-prone with ÷17, that friction is the point: it shows why an awkward divisor often calls for long division.
activities.rationale: Method choice may be learned effectively by doing the same division both ways and experiencing the efficiency/reliability trade-off, with support for the mental multiples that short division compresses. Securing both methods first, then giving mixed problems where the learner decides and justifies, is proposed to build the judgement the Year 6 standard targets.

Compare the two side by side and state which was quicker for THIS divisor and why.
Now try a divisor many learners find awkward, e.g. 4080÷17, by short division; notice whether and where holding multiples of 17 mentally becomes error-prone.
Solve 4080÷17 again by long division and compare how reliable each felt.
State a rule of thumb in your own words: when the divisor's multiples are easy to hold, short division is efficient; when they are hard, long division is safer.
Estimate first (e.g. 3600÷16 ≈ 225) and check the final answer by multiplying the quotient back (228×16 = 3648?).
activities.intendedInsight: Whether short or long division is the better tool depends on how friendly the divisor is, not on habit — and you can experience this trade-off by doing the same calculation both ways. Both methods are legitimate; the skill is choosing and justifying.

activities.title: Justify the method for a mixed set
feedback: A good justification names the divisor's friendliness, e.g. 'multiples of 15 are easy (15, 30, 45…), so short division is efficient.'
If you claimed one method is always best, revisit the awkward divisor (e.g. ÷17 or ÷29) — that case shows why judgement beats a fixed rule.
Always estimate first so a slipped step is caught (e.g. 2925÷15 ≈ 3000÷15 = 200, 5887÷29 ≈ 6000÷30 = 200; the exact answers are 195 and 203).

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder in context

In a 'how many buses?' context the remainder usually forces rounding UP; in a 'how many full boxes?' context it forces rounding DOWN.

For a different context (e.g. buses needed to carry people, or full boxes that can be filled), decide whether to round up, round down, or keep a remainder, and explain why.

activities.title: Check your understanding
feedback: For method choice, the reason matters as much as the answer: short division often fits ÷16 because its multiples are easy for many learners to hold; ÷17 is often awkward because many learners find its multiples harder to derive mentally.

constraints: Secure BOTH short and long division before asking learners to choose between them; method selection presupposes fluent execution of each.
Support mental multiples of the divisor (e.g. deriving 16×3) so the compressed short-division steps are reliable; carry/remainder errors often trace back to insecure multiplication.

Do not teach that one method is universally 'better'; the objective is choosing by the numbers. Equally, do not frame a divisor's 'friendliness' as a fixed property — it depends on which multiples the individual learner can derive quickly.

Recognition-only and fill-in items assess method appropriateness and single steps but do not elicit independent choice-and-execution on new problems; pair them with a performance task where the learner chooses and carries out a method unaided.
A static side-by-side worked comparison is a useful reference for the trade-off but cannot let the learner choose and execute on new numbers; treat it as a scaffold, not the full objective.

When interpreting remainders, the correct written form depends on the context (fraction/decimal for measurement; round up or down for discrete grouping); do not apply one remainder convention universally.

activities.title: Step-by-step long multiplication with an estimate check
feedback: If the ×tens row comes out about ten times too small, you probably dropped the placeholder zero — remember that row is 2463 groups of thirty, so it must start in the tens column; the zero holds the ones place.

If one digit of a partial product is wrong, slow down the carries: write each carry above the correct column and re-check it. Your estimate (~100000) only catches errors that change the size of the final answer; a single wrong digit can still give a plausible-looking total, so re-check each multiplication and carry directly.
If you multiplied by only one digit of 37, remember 37 = 30 + 7, so you need one row for ×7 and one for ×30.
If the answer is correct but you cannot say what each row means, link back to the area model: 2463 splits into (2463×30) and (2463×7), and the two parts recombine when you add.

Work 2463×37 by long multiplication, writing the ×ones row (2463×7 = 17241) and the ×tens row underneath.
When starting the ×tens row, write the placeholder zero in the ones column first, then multiply by 3 tens to get 73890.
Add the two rows: 17241 + 73890 = 91131, keeping the columns aligned.
Compare the final answer with your estimate of ~100000 — 91131 is in the right ballpark, so the magnitude is plausible.
At each step, check that any carry is jotted above the correct column and added into the next multiplication.

The placeholder zero is there because the second row is really ×30, not ×3. The estimate bounds the answer's size, so a lost zero shows up as a clearly wrong magnitude. A carry slip usually changes only one or two digits and can still look plausible, so it has to be caught by checking the working itself.

For a fill-in-the-blank partial product, compute it directly and confirm it is consistent with the neighbouring digits and the carries recorded.
