pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 with answers to three decimal places, understanding that the DIGITS shift position in the place-value chart (the point moves nowhere; the digits move).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.2 — explain patterns in the number of zeros / placement of the decimal point when multiplying or dividing by powers of 10; extends 5.NBT.1 (a digit in one place is 1/10 of the place to its left).
• Operational details — secure the concept that ×10 shifts every digit ONE place to the LEFT (each digit becomes ten times bigger) and ÷10 shifts every digit one place to the RIGHT; ×/÷100 = two places, ×/÷1000 = three places. The decimal point is a fixed marker of the ones place; it is the digits that travel. Zeros are placeholders that appear to fill vacated places (0.0452), never 'just add a zero'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 correctly, describing it as digits moving two places left. Tier B (10–11): 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452, inserting placeholder zeros correctly. Tier C (11): explain WHY ×10 shifts each digit one place left in terms of each digit becoming ten times its value.
bestPractices: Teach 'digits move, the point stays' explicitly and BAN 'add a zero / move the decimal point' — the add-a-zero rule fails for decimals (3.4 × 10 is not 3.40) and mispositions the point; the movement-of-digits image generalises correctly.
Use a place-value chart (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths) and physically SLIDE digit cards left/right across the columns, so the shift is enacted, not stated.
Connect ×10 and ÷10 as inverse shifts (left ↔ right) and chain them (×100 = ×10 then ×10) so the size of the shift maps to the power of ten.
Confront placeholder zeros head-on: when ÷1000 empties the ones and tenths columns, a 0 must hold each empty place (0.0452), and the leading zero before the point is written by convention.
Ground WHY in place value (5.NBT.1): a digit is worth ten times the digit one place to its right, so making a number ten times bigger moves every digit into the next-higher column.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with sliding digit cards spanning thousands to thousandths and the decimal point fixed at the ones boundary.
Left/right shift arrows annotated with the power of ten (×10 = 1 left, ×100 = 2 left, ÷1000 = 3 right).
Gattegno chart (rows of ×10 scaling) to show a digit jumping between rows as it is multiplied/divided by powers of ten.
Zoom / 'ten-times' number line to reinforce that ×10 makes the whole quantity ten times as large, not merely longer to write.
commonMisconceptions: 'Add a zero when you multiply by 10' — wrong for decimals (2.5 × 10 ≠ 2.50) and a source of place-value damage.
'Move the decimal point' — leads to moving the point the wrong way or mispositioning it; the point is fixed, the digits move.
Omitting placeholder zeros when dividing (45.2 ÷ 1000 written as 0.452 or .0452 rather than 0.0452).
Confusing the DIRECTION: multiplying making the number smaller (shifting right) or dividing making it larger.
Shifting only one digit or the wrong number of places, especially for ×/÷1000 (three places).

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 (answers up to three decimal places, with 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 as a four-decimal-place extension) by understanding that every DIGIT shifts position across the place-value chart while the decimal point stays fixed at the ones boundary. The organising principle is 'digits move, the point stays'; ×10 shifts each digit one column left (each digit becomes ten times bigger), ÷10 shifts one column right, and the number of places matches the number of zeros in the power of ten. Placeholder zeros fill vacated columns (e.g. 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452). This counters the 'just add a zero' habit, which breaks for decimals, and gives a place-value reason for 'move the point', which gets correct answers but is often learned without understanding.

activities.title: Slide the digits across a place-value chart
feedback: If a learner writes 3.456 × 100 = 3.45600, point out the value has not changed at all and the digits sit in the same columns — ask them to slide each digit two columns left instead so 3 lands in the hundreds, giving 345.6.

If 45.2 ÷ 1000 comes out as 0.452, have them count every column each digit crosses and check that each written emptied column (ones and tenths) holds a 0, giving 0.0452. If it comes out as .0452, note that the value is correct but the conventional 0 in the ones place should be written: 0.0452.
If a learner shifts the wrong way, ask whether the number should get bigger (×, shift left) or smaller (÷, shift right) and re-slide.

If the shift is in the right direction but off by one place, have them match the count to the number of zeros in the multiplier/divisor and recount; if the error repeats, check whether they are counting the decimal point or digits instead of columns.
activities.rationale: The target concept is literally a movement of digits across place-value columns, so enacting the slide (physically or on screen) with the point held fixed is intended to make 'digits move, the point stays' something the learner performs rather than recites, and dividing to a leading-zero answer forces the placeholder-zero reasoning that the 'add a zero' rule hides.

Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns from thousands down to ten-thousandths, with the decimal point marked fixed at the ones boundary (ThHTO . tenths hundredths thousandths ten-thousandths); the extra low columns are needed because 45.2 ÷ 1000 lands a digit in the ten-thousandths place.
Write 3.456 into the chart using digit cards, then multiply by 100: slide EVERY digit two columns to the LEFT in one move, keeping the point pinned in place, to land on 345.6.

Now take 45.2 and divide by 1000: slide every digit three columns to the RIGHT (the tenths digit travels into the ten-thousandths column), and write a placeholder 0 into each emptied column that is written (ones and tenths) to get 0.0452.
Say aloud for each step: 'the digits moved ___ places ___ because I multiplied/divided by ___', linking the number of places to the power of ten.
Try a target challenge: starting from 3.456, work out which single operation reaches 345.6, and which reaches 0.3456.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten moves every digit a fixed number of place-value columns while the decimal point stays put; the number of columns equals the number of zeros in the power of ten, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.

activities.title: Why ten-times moves each digit one column
feedback: If a learner treats ×10 as 'making the number longer', redirect to the quantity itself being ten times as large — 2.5 × 10 is twenty-five, not 'two point five oh'.
If they cannot say why the shift is one column, revisit that each column is ten times the one to its right, so a ten-times-bigger value lands one column left.
If they struggle to connect the power of ten to the number of places, have them break ×100 into ×10 then ×10 and count the columns.
activities.rationale: Grounding the procedure in place-value structure (each place is worth ten times the place to its right) is intended to turn a memorised rule into explained behaviour, which may support transfer to ×/÷1000 and help learners resist the 'add a zero' shortcut.
sourceClaims: Pupils explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10; a digit represents ten times the place to its right.
Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Pick a digit in a number, e.g. the 4 in 3.456 (worth four tenths), and state its value.
Explain why, when the whole number is made ten times bigger, that digit must now be worth ten times as much (four ones) and therefore move one column to the left.
Use a scaling chart or a 'ten-times' number line to show the whole quantity becoming ten times as large, not merely gaining an extra written digit.
Chain the reasoning: ×100 is ×10 then ×10, so each digit moves one column left twice — two columns in total — and connect ÷10 as the exact inverse (one column right).
activities.intendedInsight: Because each place-value column is worth ten times the column to its right, making a number ten times bigger promotes every digit into the next-higher column; this is WHY the shift happens and why ×100 shifts two columns and ÷1000 three.

activities.title: Fluency and error checks
feedback: A missing-placeholder answer (0.452 for 45.2 ÷ 1000) should prompt counting every column and filling emptied ones — 0.0452.
An 'append zeros' answer (3.45600) should prompt re-sliding the digits two columns left.

An off-by-a-factor-of-ten answer should prompt the learner to recount places against the zeros in the operator; if it recurs, check how they are counting columns rather than assuming it is only a slip.
activities.rationale: Short recognition and fill-in tasks are efficient for checking fluency and catching recurring errors, though on their own they do not build the shift image — they complement the enacted chart work rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils identify the value of each digit to three decimal places and multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank items such as 45.2 ÷ 1000 = ____ , writing all placeholder zeros, and 3.456 × 100 = ____ .
Answer direction questions: when dividing by a power of ten, which way do the digits move, and how many places for ÷1000?
Order a set of results by size, e.g. 2.5 × 10, 2.5 × 100, 2.5 × 1000, and explain the ordering by place-value shift.
Self-check each answer by counting the columns crossed against the number of zeros in the multiplier or divisor.
activities.intendedInsight: Repeated practice with answers up to three decimal places (plus the four-decimal-place extension 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452) is intended to make the power-of-ten ↔ number-of-places mapping more automatic and to surface the common errors (missing placeholder zeros, wrong direction, miscounting by one).

activities.title: Challenge the 'add a zero' habit through dialogue
feedback: If a learner cannot explain the error, have them place both 2.5 and the proposed 2.50 in a chart and compare values — they are identical, so no multiplication has occurred.
Confirm the correct answer (25) by sliding each digit one column left.
activities.rationale: Prompting a learner to diagnose a misconception out loud may consolidate understanding; this is a supporting discussion activity that can accompany, but does not replace, enacting the digit shift on a chart.
sourceClaims: Teaching 'digits move, the decimal point stays' avoids the 'add a zero / move the point' misconception that fails for decimals.
learnerActions: Consider a claim a friend might make: '2.5 × 10 = 2.50'. Explain exactly what has gone wrong and give the correct answer with reasoning.
Explain why 3.456 × 100 is not 3.45600, referring to where each digit sits in the place-value chart.
Describe, in your own words, when 'add a zero' happens to look right (whole numbers) and why it fails for decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The 'add a zero' rule is unreliable for decimals because it ignores place value. 'Move the point' gives correct answers, but used as a bare rule it hides why. Explaining the flaw is intended to strengthen the digits-move model.

constraints: Explicitly teach 'digits move, the point stays' and avoid 'add a zero' because it gives wrong results for decimals (3.4 × 10 is not 3.40). Do not lead with 'move the decimal point': it gives the same answers, but it hides the place-value reason, and the point is better treated as a fixed marker of the ones place.

Placeholder zeros must be confronted directly: when division empties columns, a 0 must hold each written vacated place (0.0452 has zeros in the ones — by convention — and tenths), and answers like 0.452 or .0452 should not pass unaddressed.
Match the number of places shifted to the power of ten (×/÷10 = one place, ×/÷100 = two, ×/÷1000 = three) and keep direction correct (× shifts left/bigger, ÷ shifts right/smaller).
Provide a chart with enough low columns for the task: 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 needs a ten-thousandths column, so the chart should extend beyond thousandths for the division example.
Recognition and fill-in tasks check fluency but do not by themselves build the shift image; pair them with enacted chart work.

Discussion/dialogue activities can surface and challenge misconceptions and can accompany the enacted chart work; they need not be treated as the only route, but the curriculum concept here centres on the learner performing the digit shift.

Paper or card digit cards used on a chart have slight physical thickness and are approximations of the abstract place-value idea; an on-screen chart with sliding digits is a model of the same relationship — both are legitimate ways to enact the shift.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 (each digit two columns left), 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 (three columns right; placeholder 0 in ones by convention and in tenths, final digit in ten-thousandths), 3.456 ÷ 1000 = 0.003456, and 2.5 × 10 = 25 are correct as stated and were checked independently.

The place-value chart must extend to ten-thousandths: 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 places its final digit (2) in the ten-thousandths column, so a chart ending at thousandths (as the original representation described) cannot hold the result. Learner text now spans thousands to ten-thousandths.

The stated objective and summary say answers 'up to three decimal places', but the flagship division example 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 yields four decimal places. The arithmetic is correct; this is an original-row inconsistency flagged for review, not a learner error.

The original row's recommendation text said 'three placeholder zeros' fill the vacated ones and tenths places for 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452; that is a slip — only two written zeros are present (the ones leading zero by convention and the tenths placeholder). The learner-facing text uses the corrected 'ones and tenths' (two zeros).

The original row's optional 'drag the point instead' toggle was not carried into learner actions: moving the point and moving the digits give the same relative result only because position is relative, which can confuse learners. It is noted here for reviewers to decide whether to include such a toggle at all.
CCSS-M 5.NBT and NCETM source claims were marked unverified in the original and remain unverified here; no new verification was performed.
The reteach prerequisite links and diagnostic structure from the assessment fields were not altered and are out of scope for this rewrite.

topic.description: Solve multi-step word problems using the four operations with whole numbers, including interpreting remainders in context; represent with equations using a letter for the unknown; check with estimation

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; solve multi-step word problems using the four operations with whole numbers, interpret remainders in context, represent with an equation using a letter for the unknown, and check with estimation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'solve problems involving … multiplication and division … and a combination of these, including understanding the meaning of the equals sign'; Y4–Y5 multi-step problems and remainder interpretation.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.3 — 'solve multistep word problems … including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using … estimation including rounding.'
• Operational details — the objective is the whole problem-solving cycle for MULTI-STEP problems: parse → plan the sequence of operations → represent with an equation using a letter for the unknown → calculate → interpret (including the remainder) → check for reasonableness via estimation and the inverse. The hard parts are holding two steps (the output of step 1 feeds step 2), choosing operations per step, and interpreting a remainder in context (52 children in minibuses of 9 → 6 buses, round UP). The bar model is the central planning tool; a letter for the unknown links to algebra.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): solve a two-step problem with support, drawing a bar model. Tier B (age 9–10): solve a multi-step problem, write an equation with a letter for the unknown, and interpret the remainder. Tier C (age 10): plan and justify the operation sequence and check reasonableness by estimation.
bestPractices: Teach the full cycle explicitly — understand, plan, represent, solve, interpret, check — rather than jumping to compute; use the bar model to plan multi-step structure.
Require an equation with a letter for the unknown, bridging the problem to algebraic notation and the relational equals sign.
Make remainder interpretation a deliberate step (round up/down/keep/fraction) tied to what the context demands.
Insist on an estimate up front and a reasonableness check at the end (does the answer make sense; does the inverse confirm it?).
Use problems where the output of step 1 is needed for step 2, so children learn to carry intermediate results.
keyRepresentations: Bar model — planning and structuring multi-step problems
Equation with a letter for the unknown (n) — abstracting the plan
Number line / rounding — estimation and reasonableness check
Context frames for remainder interpretation (buses, bags, sharing)
commonMisconceptions: Doing only one step of a multi-step problem, or losing the intermediate result.
Interpreting the remainder wrongly for the context (rounding down the minibus count).
Key-word guessing the operation instead of reasoning from structure.
Not checking reasonableness, so magnitude/step errors go unnoticed.
Writing an equation that doesn't match the problem, or misusing '=' operationally across multiple steps.

activities.title: Deciding the remainder: contrasting contexts
feedback: If you treated both remainders the same way and got one wrong, ask: what physically happens to the 7 leftover children in THIS story?
If you left the answer as '5 r7', remember the question asked for whole minibuses or whole teams — 'r7' is not an answer to what was asked.

If the rounding logic was right but the quotient wrong, do not relearn interpretation — check the division with multiplication and addition (5×9 = 45 and 45 + 7 = 52; 6×9 = 54 is enough seats for all 52) and your estimate.
activities.rationale: Using two problems with identical arithmetic (52÷9 = 5 r7) but opposite remainder treatments forces interpretation to be driven by meaning in context, directly targeting fixed-rule and bare-remainder misconceptions.

learnerActions: Solve '52 children go on a trip in minibuses that hold 9 each — how many minibuses are needed?' Compute 52÷9 = 5 remainder 7.
Decide what the leftover 7 means here: the 7 children still need transport, so round UP to 6 minibuses.
Now solve the contrasting problem 'How many teams of 9 can you make from 52 children?' with the same arithmetic 52÷9 = 5 remainder 7.
Decide what the leftover means here: 7 children cannot form a full team, so the answer is 5 teams (drop the remainder).
State a sensible real-world answer each time — not 'r7' — and explain why the identical division is rounded differently; consider whether '5 and a bit' minibuses could ever make sense, and why not.
activities.intendedInsight: The same division can have opposite remainder treatments depending on the situation; you must interpret the leftover against what the context demands rather than apply a fixed rule or leave a bare remainder.

activities.title: Check and match: operation choice, equation and estimate

If you picked an unreasonable estimate, round each quantity and ask what size the answer should be.

activities.title: Socratic problem partner
feedback: If you jump to compute, your partner should ask what must be found first and why.
If you report a bare remainder, your partner should press for the real quantity the question asked for.
activities.rationale: A questioning partner can pose rich contexts and probe planning and interpretation; it supports but does not replace constructing and manipulating the bar models and equations.
learnerActions: Work with a partner (teacher, peer, or role-play character such as a trip organiser or shopkeeper) who poses a multi-step problem.
Answer probing questions aloud: 'What do we work out first?', 'What does the leftover mean here?', 'So how many buses do we actually need?'
Talk through your plan and remainder decision before committing to a final numeric answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the plan and the meaning of a remainder out loud is intended to build the reasoning and interpretation that underlie correct multi-step answers.

activities.title: Worked exemplar gallery (reference scaffold)
feedback: If you can follow the exemplar but stall on a new problem, revisit which step produced the intermediate result and how it fed the next step.
Treat the gallery as a reference: the skill is parsing and planning new problems, not recognising familiar ones.
activities.rationale: A worked gallery is a useful reference for structure, but mastery requires parsing new problems and building plans independently, so it is positioned as a scaffold.
learnerActions: Study annotated two-step exemplars that reveal each step in turn, including the bar model and the remainder decision.
For each exemplar, predict the next step before revealing it, then compare your reasoning.
After reviewing, apply the same approach to a NEW problem you have not seen worked.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing the structure of fully worked multi-step solutions, including how remainders are decided, is intended to provide a model that can support transfer to fresh problems.

constraints: Use multi-step problems where step 1's output is genuinely needed for step 2, so learners practise holding and carrying intermediate results — the core difficulty of the objective. The single-step pencil/cost problem does not serve this purpose and should be used only for operation-choice practice.
Require a real-world answer to remainder problems (whole minibuses, whole teams, or a justified fraction/decimal); a bare 'r7' is not an acceptable final answer.
Do not teach a fixed remainder rule ('always round up' or 'always drop'); the treatment must be driven by the specific context.
Require an estimate up front and a reasonableness/inverse check at the end, not only a computed number.

Recognition and matching tasks (quiz-style) can check operation choice, equation-matching and estimation and can be used during teaching, but they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a plan or bar model.
Discussion and worked-exemplar activities support reasoning and provide models but do not substitute for the learner independently building bar models and equations on new problems.

Optional interactive supports — a bar-model builder that carries the intermediate result forward, a context-interpreter where the learner sets round up / drop / keep / fraction to match the story (e.g. dragging in a 6th bus to seat the stranded 7 children), an equation strip for placing a letter for the unknown, and an estimate meter that flags unreasonable answers (e.g. an answer of '5 r7' or '5.8 minibuses', or a total cost far from the estimate) — make the mechanism concrete but are illustrative, not required.

Legacy confidence was 'high' but two of three sources were marked verified:false (CCSS-M 4.OA.3 and the NCETM/IES-WWC guidance); do not treat the cited standards or efficacy claims as independently re-checked here.

The original row (evidence and errorPatterns) labelled the pencil/cost problem 'two-step', but as worded it requires only 5 × £1.50; it is retained accurately as single-step operation-choice practice, and a genuine two-step example is supplied for the carry-the-intermediate-result activity.

The original recommendation framed rounding up as 'felt as a physical necessity, not a rule'; retained as a motivating context experience but worded as interpreting the leftover against the context, since the claim of superior efficacy over other presentations is not source-established.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11y; divide up to 4-digit ÷ 2-digit using formal long division, interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y6 'divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit whole number using the formal written method of long division, and interpret remainders as whole number remainders, fractions, or by rounding, as appropriate'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.2 — 'fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm' (Grade 6); 5.NBT.6 develops division by 2-digit divisors with models.
• Operational details — the new demand over short division is the TWO-DIGIT divisor: the child can no longer rely on recalled facts and must ESTIMATE how many times the divisor fits at each step (4752÷13: how many 13s in 47? ~3), multiply back, subtract, bring down. Building a 'menu' of helpful multiples of the divisor (13×1…×9, or chunk via 13×10=130) scaffolds the estimation. Remainder interpretation extends to expressing as a fraction (r/divisor) or decimal, or rounding by context. Chunking (partial-quotients) is a valid, more transparent bridge to the compact algorithm. Estimate first and check by multiplying back.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): long division with a small 2-digit divisor via a multiples menu, no remainder. Tier B (age 10–11): 4-digit ÷ 2-digit (4752÷13) with the remainder expressed as a fraction. Tier C (age 11): interpret the remainder three ways for three contexts and explain each long-division step.
bestPractices: Scaffold the estimate-at-each-step with a 'menu' of the divisor's multiples (or chunking/partial-quotients), since 2-digit divisors aren't in recalled facts.
Use chunking (partial quotients: subtract 13×100, 13×10…) as a transparent bridge before/beside the compact algorithm.
Interpret remainders flexibly — whole number, fraction (r/divisor), decimal, or rounded — according to context.
Estimate the quotient first (4752÷13 ≈ 4800÷12 = 400) to anchor the leading digit and catch place errors.
Always check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder.
keyRepresentations: Long-division layout with the divisor's multiples menu alongside
Chunking / partial-quotients layout (repeated subtraction of multiples)
Bar model / number line for remainder interpretation
Estimation and inverse-check (quotient×divisor + remainder)
commonMisconceptions: Poor estimation of how many times the divisor fits, then repeated correction or errors.
Place-value errors in the quotient (dropping a place when the divisor doesn't fit).
Mishandling the remainder — wrong fraction denominator, or wrong rounding direction for the context.
Bring-down/subtraction slips propagating through the calculation.
Not checking with multiplication, so errors persist.

learn.summary: For 10–11 year-olds dividing up to 4-digit numbers by a 2-digit divisor with formal long division, and interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions (remainder/divisor), decimals, or by rounding to suit context. The new demand over short division is the 2-digit divisor: the child can no longer recall facts and must estimate how many times the divisor fits at each step, so a 'menu' of the divisor's multiples (and chunking/partial-quotients) scaffolds that estimation. Estimate first, multiply back, subtract, bring down, and check by inverse multiplication.

activities.title: Long-division workbench with a multiples menu (4752÷13)
feedback: If the quotient has the wrong number of digits (e.g. 35 or 3605), check that every brought-down digit produced a quotient digit — write a 0 when 13 does not fit, and align each quotient digit above the digit being divided.
If estimation stalls or uses random multipliers, jot or consult the multiples menu (13, 26, 39, 52, 65…) and read off how many fit.
If the remainder fraction is inverted (13/7) or left as a bare 'r7', name it: 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more group, so the fraction is 7/13 — the remainder always goes over the divisor.

If one step is wrong from a subtraction/multiplication slip, don't restart the method: check your own quotient × 13 + remainder against 4752, compare with the estimate (between 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so between 300 and 400), then find and fix the faulty step.
activities.rationale: A live multiples menu supports the hardest part — estimating the quotient digit for a non-table divisor — and multiply-back/subtract with immediate flagging turns error-prone estimation into guided, self-correcting practice. Standards require interpreting the remainder as whole number, fraction, or by rounding.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long division and interpret remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
A multiples menu / chunking scaffolds quotient estimation for 2-digit divisors; remainders interpreted as fraction, decimal or rounded by context.
learnerActions: Set up 4752 ÷ 13 in the long-division layout.
Before dividing, build a side menu of multiples of 13 (13, 26, 39, 52, 65, 78, 91, 104, 117) to consult when estimating each quotient digit.

At each step, use the menu to decide how many 13s fit (e.g. 'how many 13s in 47?' → 3 because 39 ≤ 47 < 52), write that quotient digit above the correct column, multiply back, subtract, then bring down the next digit.

If the working number after bringing down is ever smaller than 13, write a 0 in the quotient for that place and bring down the next digit. This does not happen in 4752 ÷ 13 (the working numbers are 47, 85 and 72), so practise it on an example such as 3913 ÷ 13 = 301.
Finish with the remainder 7, then reframe it three ways: as the fraction 7/13 (remainder over divisor), as a decimal continuation (≈365.54), and rounded to suit a context.
Check the whole answer by computing 365×13 + 7 and confirming it equals 4752.
activities.intendedInsight: Long division by a 2-digit divisor is a repeating estimate–multiply–subtract–bring-down cycle; a multiples menu replaces the recalled facts you no longer have, and the same single division can yield several correct answers depending on how the remainder is interpreted.

activities.title: Chunking (partial quotients) as a transparent bridge
feedback: If the chunks don't add up to the compact quotient, check the place value of each chunk (hundreds, tens, ones) and that you kept subtracting while a value of 13 or more remained.
If chunks feel random, start with the largest hundreds multiple that still fits (13×300 = 3900 ≤ 4752, but 13×400 = 5200 is too big), then the tens multiple, then ones.
activities.rationale: Partial-quotients/chunking is a valid, more transparent bridge to the compact algorithm, exposing the place-value structure that compact long division compresses.
sourceClaims: A multiples menu / chunking scaffolds quotient estimation for 2-digit divisors; remainders interpreted as fraction, decimal or rounded by context.
learnerActions: Solve 4752 ÷ 13 by repeatedly subtracting easy multiples of 13: subtract 13×300 = 3900 (leaving 852), then 13×60 = 780 (leaving 72), then 13×5 = 65 (leaving 7), keeping a running tally of how many 13s you have removed.
Add the chunk counts (300 + 60 + 5 = 365) to get the quotient, with 7 left over.
Line up the chunking record beside the compact long-division layout and match each compact step to a bundled chunk.
activities.intendedInsight: The compact long-division digits are shorthand for subtracting bundles of the divisor (here 13×300, 13×60, 13×5, which give the hundreds, tens and ones digits of the quotient), so the algorithm is repeated subtraction organised by place value, not a magic routine.

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder for three contexts
feedback: If the rounding direction is wrong, re-read the context: 'buses needed' forces rounding up because the 7 leftover people still need a whole extra bus, whereas 'complete groups made' rounds down because the leftover 7 cannot make a full group.
If the fraction denominator is wrong, remember the remainder is written over the divisor (7/13), because 7 is left out of the 13 needed for one more.
activities.rationale: Remainder interpretation extends Y5 work to fractions/decimals and rounding by context, a core explicit requirement of the standard. A context dialogue or debate about the leftover's meaning may support the interpretation judgement.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils divide up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal long division and interpret remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate.
learnerActions: Take the result 4752 ÷ 13 = 365 remainder 7 and express the remainder three ways: as the fraction 7/13, as a decimal (≈0.54, giving ≈365.54), and as a rounded whole number.

Match each interpretation to a context: e.g. sharing a divisible quantity such as 4752 g of flour equally into 13 bags (fraction/decimal), versus a context where you must round up (e.g. how many buses/containers are needed), versus one where you round down (e.g. complete full groups made).
State and justify which interpretation each context demands and why rounding up or down fits.
activities.intendedInsight: One division can give several correct answers; the context decides whether the leftover is a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding up or down.

activities.title: Check and explain each step
feedback: If the estimate and the answer differ wildly, a quotient digit or a zero place is probably misplaced — recheck alignment.
If the inverse check fails, a subtraction or multiplication slip occurred in one step; find and fix that step rather than restarting.
activities.rationale: Estimating to anchor the leading digit and checking by inverse multiplication catch the classic quotient-placement and slip errors; voicing a step reveals genuine understanding of the algorithm.
learnerActions: Estimate the quotient before dividing (e.g. 13×300 = 3900 and 13×400 = 5200, so 4752÷13 is between 300 and 400; 4800÷13 ≈ 370 is a closer estimate, while 4800÷12 = 400 is a rougher overestimate) to anchor the leading digit.

After completing the division, voice what one specific step does — e.g. 'when I bring down the 5, what number am I now dividing by 13?' (answer: the brought-down value, here 85, since 47÷13 left 8 and the 5 comes down beside it).
Verify the full result by multiplying quotient×divisor and adding the remainder (365×13 + 7 = 4752).
activities.intendedInsight: Estimating first catches place-value errors, and multiplying back verifies the answer; being able to say what each step does distinguishes understanding from copying a routine.

constraints: Fraction, decimal, and rounded interpretations of the remainder must all be practised, not just a whole-number remainder; the context determines which is appropriate.
Chunking/partial-quotients is a legitimate method and transparent bridge, not just a crutch to discard; keep it available alongside the compact algorithm.
A multiples menu is a scaffold for estimation; the goal is for the child eventually to estimate quotient digits reliably, including writing a 0 when the divisor doesn't fit a brought-down value.

A tap-to-reveal worked example or multiple-choice item can serve as a reference or assessment, but recognition/reveal formats do not by themselves elicit the child's own estimation and self-correction cycle; include construction where the child does the dividing.
Always require an inverse check (quotient×divisor + remainder) so slips are caught rather than propagated.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: solve problems that require answers to be ROUNDED to a specified degree of accuracy — rounding a computed (often decimal) result appropriately for the question or context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): pupils 'solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy' and 'determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 5.NBT.4 (round decimals to any place) applied within 4.OA.3-style problem solving; SMP MP6 (attend to precision) frames choosing accuracy.
• Operational details — two intertwined skills: (i) rounding a result to a stated place (round 3.6875 to 1dp → 3.7), and (ii) deciding the SENSIBLE degree of accuracy from context, including cases where mathematical rounding must be overridden — money to the nearest penny, but 'how many containers hold the juice?' means rounding UP regardless of the digit (3.2 containers → 4). The child computes, then interprets: round conventionally, round up for 'enough', round down for 'how many complete', keep exact for money.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): compute a division and round to a specified decimal place. Tier B (10–11): choose the appropriate accuracy for a measurement/money context and round accordingly. Tier C (11): solve a problem where the unrounded decimal must be interpreted against context (whole containers needed → round up even though the digit says round down).
bestPractices: Distinguish ROUNDING RULES (nearest, by the following digit) from CONTEXTUAL rounding (round up for 'enough', down for 'complete whole units') — the classic buses/containers problems where the maths rule is deliberately overridden.
Round only at the END: teach children to keep full precision through a multi-step calculation and round the final answer, to avoid accumulated rounding error.
Use money and measures as the natural home: 'to the nearest penny' (2dp), 'to the nearest 10th of a second', so degree of accuracy is a real, purposeful decision.
Pair every rounded answer with the question 'does this level of accuracy make sense here?' — connecting to estimation/appropriate-accuracy (mt_ilPrU0cbtT) and to what the answer will be used for.
Rehearse the three context moves explicitly with sorting tasks: which problems round up, which round down, which round to nearest — so children choose the move by meaning, not habit.
keyRepresentations: Number line with the answer marked between the two candidate rounded values and the midpoint, to justify nearest-value rounding.
Context decision card: the problem, the raw answer, and a choice of round up / down / nearest with the reason.
Place-value view highlighting the digit being rounded and the deciding digit to its right.
Real-world icons (coins to the penny, containers that must be whole) anchoring why context overrides the plain rule.
commonMisconceptions: Applying the nearest-value rule when context demands rounding up ('need 3.2 buses' → answering 3 instead of 4) or down ('how many whole boxes fill' → rounding up wrongly).
Rounding at intermediate steps and accumulating error into the final answer.
Rounding to the wrong place, or using the wrong deciding digit (looking two places along).
Giving impossible precision for the context (money to 3dp, a count of people as a decimal).
Truncating (chopping digits) instead of rounding, e.g. 3.68 to 1dp given as 3.6.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: solving problems whose answers must be rounded to a specified degree of accuracy, AND deciding the sensible degree of accuracy from context. Two intertwined skills: (i) rounding a computed result to a stated place using the deciding digit (e.g. 3.6875 to 1 d.p. → 3.7), and (ii) judging from the situation when the plain nearest-value rule must be overridden — round UP for 'how many are needed/enough' (3.2 containers → 4), round DOWN for 'how many complete whole units', keep to the penny for money, keep whole for counts of people. Keep full precision through multi-step work and round only at the end.

activities.title: Round it right: scenarios where the rounding move has consequences
feedback: If a child rounds to the nearest whole (5 buses), ask what happens to the extra 5 people; a 'how many are needed to fit everyone' question rounds UP whenever the division leaves any remainder, however small the decimal part.
If a child rounds a 'how many complete units' problem up, ask whether a partial unit actually counts as a completed one — if not, round DOWN.
When the child correctly rounds up to 6 even though the decimal (.33) is below .5, name the reasoning: 'you rounded by the meaning of the problem, not by the deciding digit.'
For 47 ÷ 6 = 7.833..., confirm the deciding digit (the second decimal, 3, which is below 5) sends 7.83 down to 7.8 at one decimal place.
activities.rationale: Choosing and seeing the consequence of a rounding move is intended to make contextual rounding concrete, which is the central judgement in this problem-solving objective rather than rule recitation.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Compute a problem that yields a raw decimal, e.g. 80 people needing 15-seat buses: 80 ÷ 15 = 5.33 (to 2 d.p.).
Choose a rounding move — round to the nearest whole, round down, or round up — and, where relevant, to which place.
Play out or describe the result of your choice in the situation: rounding to the nearest whole (5 buses) seats only 75 and leaves 5 people stranded at the kerb; rounding up to 6 buses seats everyone.
State in words why context (needing to carry everyone), not the deciding digit, forces rounding up here: the deciding digit (the 3 in 5.33) would round down to 5, yet the situation needs 6.
Repeat with a 'round down' context, e.g. 'How many complete 50 cm lengths can be cut from 3.4 m?' 340 ÷ 50 = 6.8 → 6 complete lengths, not 7, even though 6.8 is nearer to 7.
Repeat with a 'nearest' context where the plain rule does apply, e.g. 'round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place' → 7.8.
activities.intendedInsight: The context — what the answer is used for — decides whether you round up, down, or to the nearest, and this can override the mechanical nearest-value rule.

activities.title: Number-line rounder for the pure mechanic
feedback: If a child gives 3.68 to 1 d.p. as 3.6, point out they chopped rather than rounded: 3.68 is past the midpoint 3.65, so it rounds up to 3.7.
If a child looks two places along for the deciding digit, refocus them on the single digit immediately to the right of the rounding place.
For a borderline value with 5 in the deciding place, state the convention used (5 or more rounds up) and rehearse a few such cases.
activities.rationale: A visual number-line placement with the deciding digit highlighted supports the standard rounding mechanic and directly confronts truncation and wrong-place errors.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
learnerActions: Mark the raw answer on a number line between the two candidate rounded values, with the midpoint shown.
Identify the digit being rounded and the deciding digit immediately to its right.
Decide which candidate the value is nearer to and round to it.
Deliberately contrast rounding with truncating: show that 3.68 to 1 d.p. is 3.7, NOT 3.6 (chopping).
activities.intendedInsight: Nearest-value rounding is justified by position on the number line and the single deciding digit; truncating (chopping digits) is a different, incorrect move.

activities.title: Money and measures: choosing a sensible degree of accuracy
feedback: If a child gives money to 3 d.p., ask what 0.001 of a pound would be in coins — there is no such coin, so round to the penny.
If a child reports a count of people as a decimal, ask how you could have part of a person; counts stay whole.
Praise reasoning that ties the chosen accuracy to how the answer is used.
activities.rationale: Money and measures give authentic reasons for choosing accuracy, making 'degree of accuracy' a real decision.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy.
Pupils round decimals to any place and attend to precision, applying rounding within problem solving.
learnerActions: For a money result, round to the nearest penny (2 d.p.) and explain why 3 d.p. is not sensible for pounds and pence.
For a measurement context, round to the stated accuracy, e.g. nearest tenth of a second.
For a count of people, give a whole number and explain why a decimal count is impossible.
For each context, answer the question: 'Does this level of accuracy make sense here, and what will the answer be used for?'
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate degree of accuracy is a purposeful decision set by the context and the use of the answer, not an arbitrary number of decimal places.

activities.title: Sort the problems: up, down, or nearest
feedback: If a child sorts by surface words rather than meaning, ask what the answer is being counted for.
Check that each sorting decision is matched by a stated reason, not just a category guess.
activities.rationale: Explicit sorting with reasons rehearses the three context moves and separates meaning-driven choice from reflex; on its own a sort checks classification rather than eliciting the full compute-then-interpret performance.
sourceClaims: Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Read a set of word problems and sort each into 'round up', 'round down', or 'round to nearest'.
For each, write the reason in words (e.g. 'need enough to fit everyone' → up; 'how many complete' → down; 'to the nearest tenth' → nearest).
Then solve two or three and carry out the move you sorted it into.
activities.intendedInsight: Children should choose the rounding move by the meaning of the problem, not by habit.

activities.title: Round at the end, not in the middle
feedback: If the two answers differ, ask the child to locate where the early rounding introduced the discrepancy.
Reinforce that the specified accuracy applies to the final answer, not to the working.
activities.rationale: Working the calculation both ways is intended to let the learner see accumulated error for themselves, which may motivate the 'round last' habit more concretely than simply being told it.
sourceClaims: Context can require rounding up ('enough') or down ('complete units') irrespective of the standard nearest-value rule, and answers should be rounded only at the end to avoid accumulated error.
learnerActions: Work a multi-step calculation twice: once rounding each intermediate value early, once keeping full precision and rounding only the final answer.
Compare the two final answers and describe whether and how early rounding changed the result (choose numbers where it does, so the effect is visible).
State the rule: keep precision through the steps, round last.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding at intermediate steps can accumulate error; rounding only the final answer protects accuracy.

activities.title: Justify-the-accuracy discussion
feedback: If the child cannot explain why 5.2 coaches rounds up to 6, revisit that 0.2 of a coach still carries 10 people who need seats (0.2 × 50 = 10).
If the child says the answer never changes with re-wording, contrast 'coaches needed' (round up to 6) with 'nearest whole number' (5.2 → round to 5).
activities.rationale: Spoken Socratic reasoning targets the judgement aspect of choosing accuracy and surfaces whether the choice is understood or habitual; a discussion can prompt justification but does not by itself confirm the child can compute and round a fresh problem.
learnerActions: Given a real situation posed aloud, say whether you would round up, down, or to the nearest, and why, BEFORE the outcome is revealed.
Answer probing questions: 'Why round UP to 6 coaches even though 5.2 is nearer 5?'; 'If the question asked for the nearest whole number instead of coaches needed, would your answer change?'
Defend your chosen degree of accuracy in words.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the accuracy decision in context — and recognising that re-wording the question can change the correct move — shows command of the objective.

constraints: A sorting/categorisation or multiple-choice format can rehearse and check which rounding move fits, but on its own it does not require the learner to carry out the full compute-then-interpret problem or explain the reasoning — pair it with worked problems and justification.
A static number-line reference supports the rounding mechanic but does not let learners play out contextual consequences; use it alongside scenario and discussion work.
Treat animated scenario outcomes as one way to make consequences visible; the same insight can come from drawing, acting out, or discussing what happens to the extra people/units.
Distinguish arithmetic slips from rounding misconceptions: if the rounding logic is right but the division is wrong, have the child recompute and re-round rather than reteaching rounding.

Choose scenario numbers so the intended teaching point is genuine: to show context overriding the plain rule, a 'round up' context needs a fractional part below .5 (e.g. 5.33 → 6 needed), and a 'round down' context needs a fractional part of .5 or more (e.g. 6.8 → 6 complete lengths); otherwise the rule and the context agree and no override is demonstrated.

The ORIGINAL row used 74 ÷ 15 = 4.93 for the override lesson, but 4.93 rounds up to 5 by the plain rule anyway, so it does not separate rule from context; the original 'close to 5 for a different reason' phrasing is muddled and was replaced.

'Round half up' is stated as the convention; some curricula/contexts use round-half-to-even. Confirm the convention against the intended standard before teaching borderline (deciding-digit 5) cases.
Efficacy framing: activity rationales were softened to intended/may wording because these are unvalidated proposals; no empirical effectiveness or human review has been established.

probeDeeper: Why do you round UP to 6 coaches even though 5.2 is nearer 5?
To round 47 ÷ 6 to one decimal place, which digit decides whether you round up or down?
When is it right to round to the nearest, and when must you round up no matter what?
If the question asked for the nearest whole number instead of coaches needed, would your answer change?
assess.correctAnswer: 47 ÷ 6 = 7.83..., to 1 d.p. = 7.8. Coaches: 260 ÷ 50 = 5.2, but you need 6 coaches (the 0.2 of a coach still carries people, so round UP). The teacher watches for correct rounding-rule application AND context-driven rounding that overrides the rule when whole units are required.

errorPatterns.pattern: applies 'round to nearest' mechanically in the coaches context — 5.2 rounds to 5, stranding people
errorPatterns.nextMove: ask what happens to the extra 10 people; a real 'how many needed' context always rounds UP to fit everyone, regardless of the decimal.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 5 coaches; child rounds down because 5.2 is nearer 5

errorPatterns.pattern: rounds to the wrong place, or rounds the intermediate value too early distorting the result
errorPatterns.nextMove: round only the FINAL answer to the specified place; identify the digit that decides the rounding.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer given to the wrong decimal place, or rounded mid-calculation causing error

errorPatterns.pattern: uses the round-half-up rule inconsistently — unsure what to do with a 5 in the deciding place
errorPatterns.nextMove: state the convention (deciding digit 5 or more rounds up) and rehearse a few borderline cases.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child hesitates or rounds 7.85-type values inconsistently

errorPatterns.pattern: rounds correctly, arithmetic slip in the division
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach rounding; have the child recompute the division and re-round.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: right rounding logic, wrong quotient

responseLevels.gap: rounds mechanically to nearest even in a 'how many needed' context (stranding people), or rounds to the wrong place.
responseLevels.full: rounds the final answer to a specified accuracy correctly AND rounds up/down as the context demands, explaining why the context governs the choice.
responseLevels.partial: applies the rounding rule correctly when asked for a decimal place but doesn't let context override it (or vice versa).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child problems where the rounding decision matters and watch how they round the RESULT: 'Work out 47 ÷ 6 and give the answer to one decimal place'; and a context one — '260 people travel in coaches holding 50 each. How many coaches are needed?' Watch whether they round by the rule when asked, but round UP for whole coaches regardless of the decimal.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The two items pull in opposite directions: one wants the rounding rule (7.83→7.8), the other wants rounding UP against the rule (5.2→6 coaches). A child who always applies 'round to nearest' answers 5 coaches and strands 10 people. Watching both reveals whether they let context govern accuracy — the objective's core.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Factors, multiples, and primes
topic.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100; identify common factors and common multiples of two numbers; use these concepts to solve problems
evidence: State the first five multiples of 7
Find the common factors of 24 and 36
Find all common factors of 36 and 48
Identify the first three common multiples of 6 and 8
Determine whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime and justify the reasoning
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} list all the factor pairs for a number like 36 — (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9), (6, 6) — and find factors that two numbers share?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11y; find all factor pairs for numbers 1–100; identify common factors and common multiples of two numbers; use these to solve problems.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'identify multiples and factors, including finding all factor pairs of a number, and common factors of two numbers'; Y6 extends to common factors/multiples.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 (all factor pairs 1–100, factor vs multiple, prime/composite) and 6.NS.4 (common factors and multiples, GCF/LCM).
• Operational details — the concepts interlock: FACTORS divide into a number (found systematically in pairs, stopping at the square root); MULTIPLES are in a number's times table (infinite). COMMON factors/multiples are shared between two numbers — the intersection. The key discriminations are factor vs multiple (goes-into vs times-table) and the systematic search that guarantees completeness. Represent factors as rectangle dimensions and multiples as number-line hops; common factors/multiples as the overlap of two such sets (a Venn/two-column tool). This is the direct foundation for simplifying fractions (common factors), common denominators (common multiples), HCF/LCM and ratio.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): list all factor pairs of a number to ~50 systematically. Tier B (age 9–10): find common factors and the first common multiples of two numbers. Tier C (age 10–11): use common factors/multiples to solve a problem and explain factor-vs-multiple precisely.
bestPractices: Search factor pairs systematically (1,2,3… pairing each), stopping at the square root, using commutativity to know the set is complete.
Sharply distinguish factors (divide into the number; finite; rectangle side-lengths) from multiples (times table; infinite; number-line hops).
Represent common factors/multiples as the OVERLAP of two sets (two lists or a Venn diagram) so 'common' means shared.
Ground the work in problems — arranging rows, coinciding events (common multiples), sharing into equal groups (common factors) — not just listing.
Explicitly link to downstream use: common factors simplify fractions; common multiples give common denominators; both feed HCF/LCM and ratio.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — factors as side lengths (factor rainbow for completeness)
Number line / multiplication-grid rows — multiples as skip-count hops
Two-set overlap / Venn diagram — common factors and common multiples
Factor and multiple lists side by side to spot the intersection
commonMisconceptions: Confusing factors with multiples (factor of 12 vs multiple of 12).
Missing factor pairs through unsystematic searching, especially middle ones and the number itself/1.
Thinking there is a 'largest multiple' or a 'smallest factor other than 1' confusion.
Treating 'common' loosely rather than as shared between BOTH numbers.
Forgetting 1 is a common factor of every pair, or that the numbers themselves are factors.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, build the interlocking ideas of factors (numbers that divide into a whole), multiples (a number's times table), and what two numbers share in common (common factors and common multiples). Learners search factor pairs systematically (pairing 1,2,3… and stopping near the square root), sharply distinguish factor from multiple, and treat 'common' as the overlap of two sets. Work is grounded in problems and linked downstream to simplifying fractions, finding common denominators, and later HCF/LCM and ratio. A manipulable sets-and-overlap tool is proposed as the core builder, with a two-tier probe and a static reference/quiz as complementary assessment and scaffolds.

activities.title: Factors-and-multiples explorer (three linked modes)
feedback: If a middle factor pair is missed (e.g. forgetting (4,9) of 36), prompt: 'Have you tried making a rectangle with 4 along one side?' and point to the gap in the rainbow.
If the child keeps checking past the square root, show that each new pair just repeats one already found — that is why you can stop near √N.
If the child slides a non-shared factor into the Venn overlap, ask: 'Is that number in BOTH lists?' and highlight the two source lists.
When the 6-hops and 8-hops coincide, name the meeting points: '24 is the first common multiple of 6 and 8; 48 and 72 are the next two.'
When the largest number in the overlap glows (12 for 24 and 36, and again for 36 and 48), name it as the highest common factor and ask how it could help simplify a fraction like 24/36.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation and comparison of sets lets completeness and shared-ness be discovered rather than told; representing factors as rectangles and common factors/multiples as set overlaps supports the meaning of 'common' and is foundational for fractions and ratio. Live number-line hops make the first common multiple visible as a collision.
sourceClaims: Representing factors as rectangles and common factors/multiples as set overlaps supports completeness and the meaning of 'common', foundational for fractions and ratio.
learnerActions: Factor mode: for a chosen number N (e.g. 36), form every possible rectangle (array) of N counters and log each pair of side-lengths as a factor pair on a factor rainbow — e.g. (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), (6,6).
Explain how you know you have found them all: pairs are logged from the outside in, and once you reach the square root the pairs repeat, so the set is complete.

Multiple mode: set one number line to skip-count in 7 and read off the first five multiples (7,14,21,28,35); then set two adjustable number lines to skip-count in 6 and 8, watch where the hops coincide, and record the first THREE common multiples (24, 48, 72) — the first collision is at 24.

Common mode: set two numbers (e.g. 24 and 36), pour each factor list into a two-set Venn diagram, slide the shared factors into the overlap, and identify the largest shared factor (12) as the highest common factor; then repeat with 36 and 48 (shared factors 1,2,3,4,6,12, highest common factor 12).
State in words what 'common' means here: a factor or multiple shared by BOTH numbers — the intersection of the two sets.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Common' literally means the overlap of two sets; completeness of a factor list comes from systematic pairing around the square root; and the first common multiple is the first place two skip-counts collide. Factors are finite and divide into a number (rectangle side-lengths), while multiples are infinite times-table hops.

activities.title: Factor detective: prove the list is complete
feedback: If the child stops arbitrarily, ask them to show that every remaining number to test would only repeat a pair already found.
If the child claims a shared factor without checking both numbers, ask them to point to it in each list.
Reinforce vocabulary when it slips: factors divide INTO the number; multiples are the number counted up.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'have we found them all? what do these two numbers share?' builds the systematic-search habit and the meaning of 'common'. It complements the visual tool by forcing explicit justification.
learnerActions: For a given number, argue aloud or in writing that no factor has been missed: test divisibility in order (1, 2, 3, …) and pair each factor with its partner.
Justify why you can stop checking near the square root: if N = a×b, one of a or b is at most √N, so any larger factor has already appeared as a partner.
Identify what two chosen numbers share and defend your answer: which factors (and which early multiples) belong to BOTH?
activities.intendedInsight: Systematic searching plus the square-root stopping point guarantees a complete factor list, and 'common' must be justified as membership in both sets.

activities.title: Is it prime? Decide and justify the stopping point
feedback: If the child says '97 is prime because it is odd', counter: 9 is odd but 3×3 (not prime), and 2 is even but prime — parity does not decide primeness.
If the child calls 1 prime, restate the exactly-two-distinct-factors definition: 1 has only one factor.
If the child lists 97, 194, 291…, re-anchor: those are multiples of 97; primeness is about what divides INTO 97.
If the child checks every number up to 96, show that factors pair up so testing primes to ~10 suffices.
activities.rationale: Asking why a learner can stop checking exposes whether they understand that factors come in pairs around the square root — the deep idea — and distinguishes a reasoner from a guesser. Common errors (prime = odd, 1 is prime, confusing factors with multiples) are directly addressed with counterexamples.
learnerActions: Decide whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime.
Test divisibility only by primes up to the square root (for 97: 2, 3, 5, 7, since √97 ≈ 9.8) and record the results.
Explain WHY you can stop at about 10: beyond √97 any factor would pair with one already checked.
Conclude using the definition: a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only one factor.
activities.intendedInsight: Primeness is about the NUMBER of factors, not about being odd; factor-pairing around the square root tells you when it is safe to stop checking.

activities.title: Static reference and checking quiz
feedback: For sorting errors, remind: factors divide into the number; multiples are in its times table.
For a wrong first-common-multiple choice, return to the two skip-counts and find the first collision (24 for 6 and 8).
Use the tap-to-reveal Venn to confirm which factors are truly shared.
activities.rationale: Listing all factors, first multiples, and common factors/multiples is crisply checkable with distractors targeting the classic factor-vs-multiple confusion; a static rainbow and Venn make completeness and overlap visible as a reference. A sort of this kind can check the factor/multiple classification but does not itself require the learner to perform the systematic search or vary the two numbers from scratch.
learnerActions: Study a factor rainbow of 36 and an adjacent Venn of the factors of 24 and 36, tapping to reveal the common factors.
Sort items into 'factor of 24' vs 'multiple of 24' to rehearse the core discrimination.
Fill in a missing factor pair of 36.
Choose the first common multiple of 6 and 8 from options and explain the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates and checks the factor/multiple distinction, completeness, and the meaning of overlap once the ideas have been built.

constraints: Target age 9–11; coverage: all factor pairs for numbers 1–100, common factors and common multiples of two numbers, and using these to solve problems, with prime/composite as a related discrimination.
Search factor pairs systematically (1,2,3… pairing each) and stop near the square root, using commutativity to confirm the set is complete.
Sharply distinguish factors (divide into the number; finite; rectangle side-lengths) from multiples (times table; infinite; number-line hops).
Treat 'common' strictly as shared between BOTH numbers (the intersection of two sets), not loosely.
Remember 1 is a common factor of every pair, the number itself is a factor, and there is no 'largest multiple'.
Define prime as exactly two distinct factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite.

Ground work in problems (arranging rows, coinciding events, sharing into equal groups), not just listing, and link explicitly to simplifying fractions (common factors), common denominators (common multiples), and later HCF/LCM and ratio.

The static rainbow/Venn and the quiz are scaffolds and checks: they let a learner read off or recognise answers but do not themselves require the learner to perform the systematic search or vary the two numbers. Use them after, or alongside, active construction.

The interactive examples (dragging counters into rectangles, adjustable number lines whose hops light up on coincidence, factor lists pouring into a Venn with the largest shared factor highlighted) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete; equivalent results can be reached with paper factor rainbows, two written multiple lists, and a hand-drawn Venn.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a 3D interactive 'poor' with the claim '3D adds cost without insight'; this universal claim is not established by catalog ratings and has been dropped rather than propagated. A manipulable 2D/physical set representation is proposed on its affordances, not on a claim that other media cannot teach the topic.

The legacy 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' fit rankings and the single 'recommended' format were catalog preferences; they are not treated as pedagogical laws. The static reference and quiz are preserved as genuine complementary tools with their stated scaffolding limits.

Worked example checked: factor pairs of 36 are (1,36),(2,18),(3,12),(4,9),(6,6) — correct and complete; √36 = 6, so (6,6) is the natural stopping pair. First five multiples of 7 are 7,14,21,28,35. First three common multiples of 6 and 8 are 24,48,72. Factors of 24 and 36 share 1,2,3,4,6,12 (HCF 12); factors of 36 and 48 share 1,2,3,4,6,12 (HCF 12). 97 is prime; testing primes up to √97 (≈9.8): 2,3,5,7 — correct stopping set.
