pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; solve ×÷ problems USING knowledge of factors, multiples, squares and cubes (e.g. is 156 a multiple of 6? which two squares sum to 100? simplify 24×25 via factor pairs).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'solve problems involving multiplication and division including using their knowledge of factors and multiples, squares and cubes'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 / 6.NS.4 (factors, multiples), 5.NBT.5–6 and 6.EE.1 (using structure/exponents) — applied within multiplicative problem solving.
• Operational details — this is the APPLICATION topic: number facts become STRATEGIC TOOLS. Three moves recur: (1) use divisibility/multiples to reason about membership ('156 a multiple of 6?' → divisible by 2 and 3); (2) use factor pairs to re-factor a hard product into an easy one (24×25 = 6×(4×25) = 6×100 = 600 — associativity + a friendly factor); (3) recall/search squares and cubes to solve puzzles (two squares summing to 100 → 36+64). The habit is to look for STRUCTURE before grinding an algorithm. Divisibility rules and the factor-rainbow support the reasoning; encourage justification.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): use a divisibility rule to test membership of a multiple. Tier B (age 9–10): simplify a product using factor pairs (16×25, 24×25) and find squares summing to a target. Tier C (age 10): choose the most efficient structural route for a calculation and justify it.
bestPractices: Frame number facts as strategic tools — re-factor a product into a friendly form (×25→×100÷4) using associativity, rather than computing directly.
Use divisibility rules (2,3,4,5,6,9,10) to reason about multiples and justify membership ('156 = even and digit-sum 12 divisible by 3, so ÷6').
Draw on the factor rainbow and known squares/cubes as a search space for puzzle-type problems.
Prompt 'is there a smarter route?' before any long calculation, building the look-for-structure habit.
Require justification and checking, not just an answer, so reasoning is explicit.
keyRepresentations: Factor rainbow / factor pairs — the re-factoring toolkit
Divisibility-rule checklist — reasoning about multiples
Array/area re-partition — showing 24×25 as 6×(4×25)
Squares/cubes list — search space for sum/target puzzles
commonMisconceptions: Grinding the standard algorithm instead of spotting a factor-pair shortcut.
Misapplying divisibility rules (e.g. thinking any even number is a multiple of 6).
Re-factoring incorrectly (breaking associativity: 24×25 ≠ 24×4×25).
Confusing factors, multiples, squares and cubes when selecting a tool.
Not justifying membership/answers, so errors go unchecked.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10: solve multiplication and division problems by USING knowledge of factors, multiples, squares and cubes as strategic tools, rather than grinding a written algorithm. Three recurring moves: (1) use divisibility rules to reason about whether a number is a multiple (e.g. is 156 a multiple of 6?); (2) re-factor a hard product into a friendly one using associativity (24×25 = 6×(4×25) = 6×100 = 600); (3) recall or search squares and cubes to solve puzzles (two squares summing to 100 → 36+64). The central habit is to scan for exploitable structure before reaching for a procedure, and to justify answers rather than just state them.

activities.title: Re-factoring: turn an ugly product into a friendly one
feedback: If a learner sets up long multiplication, prompt: 'Which two factors here make a round number?' then let them pull that factor out and re-pair it.
If a learner writes 24×25 = 24×4×25, flag that this changes the value: 24 must be split (24 = 6×4) before the 4 is moved, so it is 6×4×25, not 24×4×25.

When the re-group is correct, ask them to name the rule they used (associativity) and to sanity-check the answer against a rough estimate — e.g. round 24 up to 25, so 24×25 is a little under 25×25 = 625, which makes 600 a sensible result, confirming 6×100 = 600.
activities.rationale: Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor is an efficient strategy worth teaching explicitly; manipulating the factors can make the structural insight concrete, and in an interactive setup the total can be shown to stay constant as the grouping changes.
sourceClaims: Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor, and divisibility-rule reasoning, are efficient strategies to teach explicitly.
learnerActions: Face a product such as 24×25 and, before calculating, ask: which factors could pair up to make a round number?
Split one factor and re-group: pull a 4 out of 24 (so 24 = 6×4) and pair it with 25 to make 4×25 = 100, leaving 6×100 = 600.
Confirm the total is unchanged by the rearrangement — only the grouping changed, not the value (associativity).
Try the same move on 16×25 (= 4×(4×25) = 4×100 = 400) and other products with a friendly hidden factor.
State in words why the shortcut works and when it does NOT help (if no factor pairs to a round number).
activities.intendedInsight: A fearsome-looking product often never needs a written algorithm: spotting a friendly factor pair (like 4×25 = 100) and using associativity collapses it to a one-step mental calculation. Rearranging factors leaves the total unchanged.

activities.title: Divisibility detective: is it a multiple of 6?
feedback: If a learner says 156 is a multiple of 6 just because it is even, give the counterexample 8 (even, not a multiple of 6) and establish both conditions are needed.
If a learner relies only on the digit-sum (÷3) test, give the counterexample 9 (passes ÷3, not a multiple of 6).
If the strategy is right but the digit sum is miscalculated, do not reteach the method — ask them to re-add the digits and re-check.
activities.rationale: Using divisibility rules (2, 3, 6) to justify multiple-membership makes reasoning explicit and targets the common error of testing only one condition; a counterexample directly addresses the 'even means multiple of 6' slip.
sourceClaims: Factors/multiples (4.OA.4, 6.NS.4) and structural strategies underpin efficient multiplicative problem solving.
Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor, and divisibility-rule reasoning, are efficient strategies to teach explicitly.
learnerActions: Test whether 156 is a multiple of 6 WITHOUT long division, by checking the rule for 2 (even?) and the rule for 3 (digit sum a multiple of 3?).
For 156: it is even (passes ÷2) and its digits sum to 1+5+6 = 12, a multiple of 3 (passes ÷3), so it passes BOTH and IS a multiple of 6 (check: 6×26 = 156).
Explain why passing only one test is not enough, using a counterexample: 9 is divisible by 3 but is NOT a multiple of 6; 8 is even but NOT a multiple of 6.
Repeat with 96 (even; digit sum 9+6 = 15 → multiple of 3; so yes, a multiple of 6) and a non-example such as 100 (even but digit sum 1, not a multiple of 3 → not a multiple of 6).
Justify each verdict out loud or in writing, naming both conditions.
activities.intendedInsight: Because 6 = 2×3, a number is a multiple of 6 only if it is divisible by BOTH 2 and 3. Divisibility rules let you reason about membership and justify it without dividing.

activities.title: Squares and cubes as a search space
feedback: If a learner guesses randomly, prompt the systematic method: 'Pick a square, subtract it from 100, is what's left also a square?'

Confirm 36 + 64 = 100 and ask whether any OTHER pair of nonzero squares also works (none does; 64 + 36 is the same pair in the other order, and the only other split, 0 + 100, uses 0, which the question excludes), reinforcing the exhaustive search.
If a learner confuses a square with a cube, re-anchor: a square is n×n, a cube is n×n×n.
activities.rationale: Drawing on known squares and cubes as a deliberate search space supports puzzle-type multiplicative problems and the habit of organised reasoning.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils solve ×÷ problems using knowledge of factors and multiples, squares and cubes.
learnerActions: List the square numbers up to 100 (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100) as a search space.
Find two square numbers that add to 100 by scanning the list: 36 + 64 = 100.
Describe the search strategy used (e.g. pick a square, subtract from 100, check if the remainder is also a square) rather than guessing randomly.
Extend to a cubes puzzle, e.g. list the cubes 1, 8, 27, 64 and find a cube greater than 1 that is also a square (64 = 8² = 4³; note that 1 = 1² = 1³ is also both, as a trivial case).
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing squares and cubes turns puzzle problems into an organised search: you can systematically test candidates instead of guessing, and some numbers belong to more than one family.

activities.title: Factor or multiple? Choosing the right tool
feedback: If a learner checks whether 6 divides into small numbers when the question asks whether 156 is a multiple of 6, re-anchor: a multiple of 6 appears when counting UP in sixes.
Reward naming the chosen route and giving a reason, not just the answer.
If a learner brute-forces every problem, ask them to find one problem in the set where a factor pair or divisibility rule saves work.
activities.rationale: Confusing factors and multiples drives wrong tool selection; explicitly distinguishing the vocabulary and prompting 'is there a smarter route?' builds the look-for-structure habit the standard targets.
sourceClaims: Factors/multiples (4.OA.4, 6.NS.4) and structural strategies underpin efficient multiplicative problem solving.
Re-factoring products using associativity and a friendly factor, and divisibility-rule reasoning, are efficient strategies to teach explicitly.
learnerActions: For each problem, decide first whether it is asking about FACTORS (numbers that divide into it) or MULTIPLES (numbers you land on counting up).
Re-anchor the vocabulary with a check: multiples of 6 are what you reach counting up in sixes (6, 12, 18, ...); factors of 6 are numbers that divide into it (1, 2, 3, 6).
Classify a mixed set of tasks: 'Is 156 in the six-times sequence?' (multiple), 'What divides exactly into 24?' (factor).
After choosing a strategy for a calculation, pause on the question 'Is there a smarter route than the algorithm?' and justify the chosen route.
activities.intendedInsight: Selecting the correct tool depends on distinguishing factors from multiples; the strategic habit is to look for structure and justify the route before computing.

constraints: Multiple-choice or fill-in tasks (e.g. 'is 156 a multiple of 6?' with justification options, 'the smartest way to compute 16×25', 'two squares summing to 100') are useful for checking divisibility judgements and strategy choice, especially with distractors built from the mis-applied-rule and wrong-re-factor errors; but recognition-only responses check rather than elicit the learner's own re-grouping, so pair them with tasks where the learner constructs the re-grouping themselves.

A worked gallery of shortcut exemplars (e.g. revealing the 6×(4×25) re-group) and a divisibility-rule reference card are helpful references, but the skill requires applying structure to NEW problems, which fixed exemplars alone do not demand.

A Socratic 'is there a cleverer way than the algorithm?' dialogue can build the strategic habit and prompt justification; the re-factoring step may be clearer when learners can physically rearrange the factors themselves, though this comparative benefit is untested here.
When re-grouping a product, a factor must be split before it is moved: 24×25 = (6×4)×25 = 6×(4×25). Writing 24×4×25 changes the value and is wrong.
Require justification and checking, not just an answer, so errors (such as a miscalculated digit sum) are caught; distinguish a strategy error from an arithmetic slip and respond accordingly.

Interactive re-grouping (e.g. dragging a factor to form a round number, or a panel showing instant pass/fail against each divisibility rule) is offered as an optional way to make the mechanism concrete, not a required mechanism.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit (arithmetic): verified 24×25 = 600 via 6×100; 16×25 = 400 via 4×100; 6×26 = 156; 6×16 = 96; digit sums 1+5+6=12 and 9+6=15 (both multiples of 3); 36+64=100; 64 = 8² = 4³. All check out.

Self-audit (divisibility): divisibility by 6 requires BOTH 2 and 3. The source counterexample '9 passes ÷3 but is not a multiple of 6' is correct and retained; an even-only counterexample (8) was added so both single-condition errors are directly refuted in the activity rather than merely cautioned.

The squares-summing-to-100 search confirms 36+64 is the only nonzero pair (0+100 is degenerate); the cubes puzzle names 64 as the non-trivial cube that is also a square and flags 1 = 1² = 1³ as a trivial qualifier.
The associativity pitfall (24×25 ≠ 24×4×25) is stated in both the activity-1 feedback and a constraint: split 24 = 6×4 before moving the 4.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; know and use the vocabulary of prime, prime factor and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall primes up to 19.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors and composite numbers'; 'establish whether a number up to 100 is prime and recall prime numbers up to 19'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 — 'determine whether a given whole number in the range 1–100 is prime or composite.'
• Operational details — the definition is exact-and-fragile: a prime has EXACTLY two factors (1 and itself); composite has more than two; and 1 is NEITHER (only one factor) — a point pupils routinely get wrong. Build primeness ON factor-finding: a prime is a number whose only rectangle is 1×n (one factor pair). To test primality efficiently, check divisibility only by primes up to the square root (test 97: not ÷2,3,5,7 → prime). Divisibility rules (2,3,5,10) accelerate this. Recall of primes to 19 (2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19) should be memorised. Seeds prime factorisation, HCF/LCM.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): state the definition and list primes to 19. Tier B (age 9–10): determine whether a number like 51 is prime and justify (51=3×17 → composite). Tier C (age 10): explain why 1 is not prime and use square-root-bounded checking to test a number like 97.
bestPractices: Define prime as EXACTLY two factors and build it on factor-finding — a prime is a number with only the 1×n rectangle — so the definition is grounded, not memorised.
Address the '1 is prime' misconception head-on: 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
Teach efficient primality testing — check divisibility by primes up to the square root — supported by divisibility rules for 2, 3, 5.
Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square to reveal the primes and why multiples are composite.
Require justification ('51 = 3×17 so it's composite'), not just a prime/composite label; memorise primes to 19.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array — a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle (one factor pair)
Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square — crossing out multiples leaves the primes
Factor list / factor rainbow — counting factors to classify
Divisibility-rule checks up to the square root
commonMisconceptions: Believing 1 is prime (it has only one factor — it is neither).
Thinking all odd numbers are prime (9, 15, 21, 51 are composite) or that 2 isn't prime because it's even.
Classifying by 'feel' without checking factors/divisibility.
Checking divisibility inefficiently (testing all numbers, not just primes to the square root).
Confusing 'prime factor' with 'factor' — not every factor is prime.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning prime, prime factor and composite numbers: establish whether a number up to 100 is prime and recall the primes to 19. Primeness is grounded on factor-finding — a prime is a number whose only rectangle is 1×n (exactly two factors: 1 and itself); composite has more than two; 1 is neither because it has only one factor. Learners build this through rectangle-building, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, efficient square-root-bounded divisibility testing, and justified classification (e.g. 51 = 3×17 → composite), with checkable recall and reasoning to confirm the definition they actually hold.

activities.title: Rectangle-building: when is only 1×n possible?
feedback: If a learner calls 51 prime, prompt: try arranging the counters into 3 equal rows — do they fill? (3×17 = 51, so it is composite.)
If a learner says 1 is prime, point to the single 1×1 square: that is only one factor, and a prime needs exactly two, so 1 is neither.

When 97 forms only the 1×97 line after testing the primes up to its square root, confirm: since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested, no other rectangle is possible, so its only factors are 1 and 97 and it is prime.
activities.rationale: Building primeness on factor-finding with a concrete rectangle/array model grounds the definition rather than leaving it memorised, and lets learners see directly why 1 is neither.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: Take a number and try to arrange that many counters (or squares on grid paper) into complete rectangles with more than one row and more than one column (a single line, 1×n, does not count as another rectangle).
For 51, find that a 3×17 rectangle can be built, so 51 has factors other than 1 and itself — it is composite.

For 97, try rows of 2, 3, 5 and 7 — the primes up to its square root (just under 10), since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested — and find that only a single 1×97 line forms, so 97 is prime.
Try the number 1: it forms only a single 1×1 square — one factor — so it fits neither the prime nor the composite group.
Record each verdict with its factor pair as justification (e.g. '51 = 3×17, composite'; '97, only 1×97, prime').
activities.intendedInsight: A prime number can only be made into the 1×n rectangle (exactly two factors); a composite makes at least one other rectangle; and 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only a single factor.

activities.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square
feedback: If a learner expects to keep crossing out past 7 to find the primes under 100, note that once multiples of primes up to √100 = 10 are removed (2, 3, 5, 7), the survivors other than 1 are already prime.
If a learner crosses out 2 itself, remind them to circle (keep) the first number and cross out only its later multiples.
activities.rationale: The sieve reveals why multiples are composite and leaves the primes visible, connecting classification to divisibility structure.
sourceClaims: Prime should be defined as exactly two factors (1 is neither); the Sieve of Eratosthenes and square-root-bounded divisibility testing support efficient classification.
learnerActions: On a 1–100 grid, first cross out 1 (it is neither prime nor composite), then circle 2 and cross out every later multiple of 2.
Move to the next uncrossed number (3) and cross out its multiples; repeat for 5, then 7.

Notice that the numbers still standing (circled or uncrossed) are exactly the primes, and that every number crossed out as a multiple is a multiple of a smaller prime, so it is composite (1 was crossed out separately because it is neither).
Highlight the primes up to 19 (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19) for memorisation.
activities.intendedInsight: Composite numbers are exactly the multiples that get crossed out; once 1 is set aside as neither, the survivors are the primes. This also makes the primes to 19 visible for recall.

activities.title: Efficient primality testing to the square root
feedback: If a learner keeps testing divisors above the square root, explain that any factor larger than √n would pair with one smaller than √n, which would already have been found.
If a learner tests every number rather than just primes, note that a composite divisor (e.g. 4) is already covered by its prime factor (2).
activities.rationale: Square-root-bounded checking with divisibility rules gives an efficient, reasoned method for establishing primality rather than exhaustive trial.

learnerActions: To test whether a whole number greater than 1 is prime, divide only by the primes 2, 3, 5, 7… up to its square root (1 is neither prime nor composite, so it is not tested this way).

Test 97: not even, digit sum 16 (not divisible by 3), does not end in 0/5, not divisible by 7 — and since the next prime 11 has 11×11 = 121 > 97, there is no need to test further, so 97 is prime.

activities.title: Classify and justify, including the tricky cases

If a learner calls 9 prime, prompt 9 = 3×3, so it has a third factor (3) beyond 1 and 9, making it composite.
If a learner confuses 'prime factor' with 'factor', note that 51's factors are 1, 3, 17, 51, but its prime factors are only 3 and 17.
activities.rationale: Direct, justified classification confronts the most common misconceptions (1 is prime, odd=prime, 2 isn't prime) and distinguishes factor from prime factor.

activities.intendedInsight: Classification requires checking factors, not 'feel': parity does not decide primeness, 1 is neither, and every classification needs a factor justification.

activities.title: Prove it: Socratic justification challenge
feedback: If the learner says they must test all numbers up to 96, guide them to the square-root bound and to testing only primes.

activities.rationale: A discussion/justification task surfaces the actual definition a learner holds and builds efficient-testing reasoning; it complements the concrete rectangle and sieve work.
learnerActions: Respond to the question 'How could you prove 97 is prime without checking every number below it?' by describing which divisors you need to test and why.

constraints: A pre-made, tap-to-reveal hundred square and definition card are useful as a reference and primes-to-19 memory aid, but do not let the learner test arbitrary numbers or run the sieve themselves; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on building.

Always require a factor justification ('51 = 3×17 so composite'), not just a prime/composite label.

The definition is exact and fragile — a prime has exactly two distinct factors (1 and itself); 1 has only one factor and is neither; 2 is prime despite being even.

topic.name: Square and cube numbers
topic.description: Recognise and use square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared (²) and cubed (³)
evidence: Identify 49 as 7² and explain that 7 × 7 = 49
Calculate 4³ = 64 and explain it means 4 × 4 × 4

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³ (49 = 7² = 7×7; 4³ = 64 = 4×4×4).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'recognise and use square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared (²) and cubed (³)'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): connects to 5.NBT.2 (whole-number exponents for powers of 10) and 6.EE.1 (evaluate expressions with whole-number exponents); square/cube language is developed through area and volume.
• Operational details — the notation must be tied to its GEOMETRIC meaning: n² is the area of an n×n square (a genuinely square array), n³ is the volume of an n×n×n cube. This is where 'squared' and 'cubed' get their names — not arbitrary labels. The dangerous misconception is reading n² as n×2 (7² as 14) and n³ as n×3; anchoring to the square/cube array blocks it. Square numbers are the diagonal of the multiplication table (products of equal factors) and have an odd number of factors. Cubes require the genuinely 3D step. Recall the first ~10 squares and small cubes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): read/write ² and ³ and compute small cases (5², 2³) as repeated equal multiplication. Tier B (age 9–10): list the first ten square numbers and explain 7² as a 7×7 square. Tier C (age 10): explain why n²≠n×2, connect squares to the multiplication-table diagonal, and cubes to volume.
bestPractices: Anchor ² and ³ to their geometric meaning — n² as an n×n square's area, n³ as an n×n×n cube's volume — so the names and notation make sense.
Confront the n² = n×2 misconception directly by showing 7² (a 7×7 array of 49) next to 7×2 (14).
Locate square numbers on the multiplication-table diagonal (equal factors) and note their odd factor count.
Build cubes with unit cubes / a 3D model so 'cubed' is genuinely spatial, distinct from squares.
Memorise the first ten squares and the small cubes, and use correct notation (49 = 7², not 7×7 only).
keyRepresentations: n×n square array — area meaning of n²
n×n×n cube of unit cubes — volume meaning of n³
Multiplication-table diagonal — the square numbers
Notation cards linking 7² = 7×7 = 49 and 4³ = 4×4×4 = 64
commonMisconceptions: Reading n² as n×2 (7²=14) and n³ as n×3 (4³=12).
Confusing squared and cubed, or the notation ²/³.
Thinking of square/cube numbers as arbitrary lists rather than areas/volumes.
Believing squaring always makes a much bigger number without the geometric picture (surprised by 1²=1).
Not recognising square numbers as products of a number with itself (table diagonal).

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning to recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³ (e.g. 49 = 7² = 7×7; 4³ = 64 = 4×4×4). The central aim is to tie the notation to its geometric meaning: n² is the area of an n×n square and n³ is the volume of an n×n×n cube — this is where 'squared' and 'cubed' get their names. The most important misconception to defeat is reading the exponent as a multiplier (7² as 7×2 = 14, or 4³ as 4×3 = 12); anchoring to the square and cube arrays blocks it. Square numbers also lie on the diagonal of the multiplication table (products of equal factors) and have an odd number of factors. Learners should recall the first ~10 squares and the small cubes and use correct notation.

activities.title: Growing squares: why 7² is not 7×2
feedback: If a learner writes 7² = 14, place the 7×7 array (49 cells) next to a 7×2 rectangle (14 cells): the square obviously holds far more. Rename the exponent as 'how many 7s are multiplied', so 7² = 7×7.
If a learner is surprised that 1² = 1, show the 1×1 square — a single cell — and confirm squaring does not always make a much bigger number.
When a learner notices the gaps 3, 5, 7, affirm it: each new square adds an L-shaped border of odd size, which is why the differences are consecutive odd numbers.
activities.rationale: Building the array and comparing n² against n×2 side by side makes the area meaning concrete and directly addresses the dominant exponent-as-multiplier error. Locating squares on the multiplication-table diagonal connects the notation to equal factors.
sourceClaims: Square and cube notation should be anchored to the area of a square and volume of a cube to prevent the n²=n×2 error; squares lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.
Y5 pupils recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³.
learnerActions: Build or draw an n×n square array for a chosen n and count the total cells, writing it as n².
Start small and step n up: 1 (1 cell), 2 (a 2×2 of 4), 3 (a 3×3 of 9), 4 (a 4×4 of 16). Write each as 1², 2², 3², 4².
Build a 7×7 square (49 cells) and, beside it, a separate 7×2 rectangle (14 cells); compare the two by eye — note that 7² = 49 is far larger than 7×2 = 14.
Say out loud what the little 2 means: 'how many 7s are multiplied together', i.e. 7×7, NOT 'multiply 7 by 2'.
Notice how much is added each time n grows by one: the totals jump 1, 4, 9, 16, and the gaps are 3, 5, 7 — successive odd numbers.
Plot each square number onto the diagonal of a multiplication table (where the row number equals the column number) and see that square numbers are the products of a number with itself.

Optionally notice that a square number has an odd number of factors — e.g. 9 has factors 1, 3, 9 (three of them) — because its square root is a repeated factor that pairs with itself instead of a different partner.
activities.intendedInsight: n² means an n×n square array (its area), not n×2. The notation is a picture of a square, and square numbers are the products of equal factors that lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.

activities.title: Building a cube: what 'cubed' really means
feedback: If a learner writes 4³ = 12, build the cube by layers so the 64 cubes are visible and unmistakably more than 12; rename the exponent as 'how many 4s multiplied', giving 4×4×4.
If a learner gives 16 for both 4² and 4³, set the flat 4×4 square (16) next to the 4×4×4 solid (64): two equal factors for square, three for cube. The exponent tells which.
When a learner builds layer by layer and states 4 layers × 16 = 64, affirm the link between the stacking and n×n×n.
activities.rationale: Cube numbers are genuinely spatial, so constructing an n×n×n cube from unit cubes makes 'cubed' meaningful and clearly distinct from 'squared'. Contrasting the flat square with the solid cube separates the two operations by their number of equal factors.
sourceClaims: Square and cube notation should be anchored to the area of a square and volume of a cube to prevent the n²=n×2 error; squares lie on the multiplication-table diagonal.
Whole-number exponent notation is developed in 5.NBT.2 (powers of 10) and 6.EE.1 (evaluate expressions with exponents); square/cube meaning connects to area and volume.
learnerActions: Using unit cubes (physical or a build-it model), assemble an n×n×n cube for a chosen n, stacking it layer by layer (each layer is n×n). Keep a running total, and when all n layers are in place write the final total as n×n×n = n³.
Build 4³ specifically: make four layers, each a 4×4 square of 16 cubes, to reach 64 cubes total; write 4³ = 4×4×4 = 64.
Rotate or turn the cube to see all its faces and confirm it is genuinely three-dimensional.
Place a flat 4×4 square (16) beside the 4×4×4 cube (64) and describe the difference: squared uses two equal factors (a flat area), cubed uses three (a solid volume).
Say what the little 3 means: 'how many 4s are multiplied together' — 4×4×4 — not 'multiply 4 by 3'.
activities.intendedInsight: n³ means an n×n×n cube built from unit cubes (its volume), using three equal factors. 'Cubed' is spatial and distinct from 'squared'; the exponent counts how many equal factors are multiplied.

activities.title: Reading and recalling the notation
feedback: If a learner picks 14 for 7², treat it as the key trap: point back to the 7×7 array of 49 and restate the exponent's meaning.
If recall of a square or cube is shaky, rebuild it as repeated equal multiplication (e.g. 4³ = 4×4×4) rather than guessing.
Correct notation matters: encourage writing 49 = 7², not only 7×7, so the symbol becomes familiar.
activities.rationale: Recall and reading of notation are checkable and benefit from the exponent-as-multiplier distractor; pairing each symbol with its array/cube keeps the geometric meaning attached rather than treating the numbers as an arbitrary list. Recognition and recall practice consolidates but does not by itself build the area/volume meaning — pair it with the building activities.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils recognise and use square and cube numbers and the notation ² and ³.
learnerActions: Match notation to meaning and value: 7² ↔ a 7×7 array ↔ 49; 4³ ↔ a 4×4×4 cube ↔ 64. For each, first predict, then reveal the picture and the value.
Answer the question 'why is 7² not 14?' in your own words, referring to the 7×7 square.
List the first ten square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100) and write each with its notation (e.g. 49 = 7²).
Recall the small cubes (1³=1, 2³=8, 3³=27, 4³=64, 5³=125) and write each as repeated equal multiplication.
Write a value using correct notation, e.g. record 49 as 7² (not only as 7×7).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and correct reading of ² and ³ rest on the array/cube meaning; the notation is shorthand for repeated equal multiplication, not a multiplier.

constraints: Tie ² and ³ to geometric meaning: n² as an n×n square's area, n³ as an n×n×n cube's volume, so the names and notation make sense rather than being arbitrary labels.
Directly confront the exponent-as-multiplier error by showing 7² (a 7×7 array of 49) alongside 7×2 (14), and 4³ (64) rather than 4×3 (12).
Distinguish squared from cubed by number of equal factors (two vs three) and by shape (flat area vs solid volume).

Recognition/recall practice (matching, fill-in, multiple choice) tests and consolidates but does not by itself build the area/volume meaning — use it after or alongside construction, not instead of it.
Include 1² = 1 so learners see squaring does not always make a much larger number.

Expectations by stage: at age 9, read/write ² and ³ and compute small cases as repeated equal multiplication; by age 9–10, list the first ten squares and explain 7² as a 7×7 square; by age 10, explain why n² ≠ n×2, connect squares to the multiplication-table diagonal, and cubes to volume.

Physical unit cubes and build-it screen models offer different experiences; either can make 'cubed' spatial. A flat drawing can still show and teach the square meaning even though it cannot be dragged to vary n.

The original flagged two sources as unverified (Common Core connection to 5.NBT.2/6.EE.1, and the NCETM guidance on anchoring to area/volume and the table diagonal); only the DfE National Curriculum claim was marked verified. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

errorPatterns.nextMove: build the square: 4² is a 4×4 array = 16 tiles, visibly not 8; contrast with 4×2 = a 4×2 rectangle of 8. Name the exponent as 'how many 4s are multiplied', not 'multiply by the little number'.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 11–12: use the vocabulary and concepts of primes, factors, multiples, common factors/multiples, HCF and LCM, and PRIME FACTORISATION with index notation and the unique-factorisation property (every integer has exactly one prime-factor decomposition).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.4 (GCF and LCM, distributive use of GCF); prime factorisation and index notation formalise Grade 4 factor/multiple work (4.OA.4).
• Operational details — build a number's prime factorisation with a factor tree, record it in index form (360 = 2³ × 3² × 5), and USE factorisations to find HCF (product of shared prime powers, the lowest index of each) and LCM (highest index of each prime present). The unique-factorisation property is the conceptual anchor: however you build the tree, the prime 'fingerprint' is the same. Venn-diagram-of-primes is the canonical HCF/LCM organiser.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): express a number as a product of primes in index form via a factor tree. Tier B (11–12): find HCF and LCM of two numbers from their prime factorisations. Tier C (12): explain, via unique factorisation, why every integer has exactly one set of prime factors and why HCF×LCM = product of the two numbers.
bestPractices: Anchor on the UNIQUE FACTORISATION property by having children build the SAME number with different first splits (360 = 4×90 or 8×45) and confirm the prime fingerprint is identical — the tree branches differ, the primes don't.

Teach HCF and LCM THROUGH prime factorisation rather than as separate list-and-compare tricks: a Venn diagram of the two numbers' prime factors gives HCF (intersection product) and LCM (whole-diagram product) at a glance.
Insist on index notation as compact, meaningful shorthand (2³ not 2×2×2) and connect it to the powers/indices work (dependent mt_hCVPYlF-7Y).

Ground HCF/LCM in problems that MOTIVATE them — HCF for simplifying/sharing into equal groups, LCM for repeating-event and fraction-denominator problems — so the concepts have purpose, not just procedure.
Reinforce that 1 is neither prime nor composite and that primes are the multiplicative 'atoms', linking back to the Y5-6 primes and factor-pairs work (prerequisite mt_FHIAv6dfhU).
keyRepresentations: Factor tree branching a number down to its prime leaves, then collected into index form.
Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors: intersection → HCF, union (whole diagram) → LCM.
Index-notation product (360 = 2³ × 3² × 5) as the number's unique 'prime fingerprint'.
Prime-factor tiles/counters that can be regrouped to show different trees yield the same multiset of primes.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a number can have different prime factorisations depending on how the tree is drawn (missing the uniqueness property).
Treating 1 as prime, or including 1 in a factorisation.
Confusing HCF with LCM (taking the largest common multiple or smallest common factor), or muddling which is 'highest' vs 'lowest'.
Taking the highest index for HCF / lowest for LCM (rule reversed).
Stopping a factor tree at composite leaves (e.g. leaving 4 or 6 unfactored) so the factorisation isn't fully prime.

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: build a number's prime factorisation with a factor tree, record it in index form (e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5), and use prime factorisations to find HCF (lowest power of each shared prime) and LCM (highest power of each prime present). The conceptual anchor is the unique-factorisation property — however the tree is built, the multiset of primes is identical. A Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors organises HCF (intersection product) and LCM (whole-diagram product). Includes production, reference/anchor, consolidation, and Socratic-discussion activities, with scaffold limits noted.

activities.title: Prime factory: build the tree, discover uniqueness
feedback: If two differently built trees give different prime sets, either a leaf was left composite or a split was miscalculated (the two factors do not multiply back to the number above them) — check every split by multiplying and check that every leaf is prime, then compare again.
If a leaf like 4, 6, or 9 remains, the factorisation is not finished: 4 = 2×2, 6 = 2×3, 9 = 3×3. Split until only primes remain.
Remember that 1 is neither prime nor composite and never belongs in the factorisation.
activities.rationale: Prime factorisation is an active decomposition; building the same number two ways and seeing the identical prime set is intended to let uniqueness be discovered rather than asserted. Index notation is taught as meaningful shorthand (2³ not 2×2×2). Supported by the KS3 requirement to use product notation and the unique factorisation property; the specific method is a research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors/multiples, HCF, LCM, and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property.
learnerActions: Take a number such as 360 and repeatedly split it into a factor pair (e.g. 4 × 90), then keep splitting each branch until every leaf is a prime.
Collect the prime leaves and write them in index form: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
Now build 360 a second time starting from a different first split (e.g. 8 × 45 instead of 4 × 90). Record the prime leaves again.
Lay the two sets of prime leaves side by side and check: the trees branched differently, but the collected primes are identical (2³ × 3² × 5 both times).
Check each tree for composite leaves left unsplit (e.g. a 4 or a 9 that should become 2×2 or 3×3) and finish splitting them.
activities.intendedInsight: Every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one prime 'fingerprint': the order and shape of the splits do not change which primes (and how many of each) you end up with. Composite leaves must be fully broken down before the factorisation is complete.

activities.title: Venn organiser for HCF and LCM
feedback: If a learner gives 72 for the HCF, they took the highest power of each prime — that is the LCM. A common factor must divide BOTH numbers, so it can only use the powers BOTH have, i.e. the lowest; correct the HCF to 2² × 3 = 12.

If a learner multiplies together every prime that appears in either number, remind them a common factor must divide BOTH, so a prime appearing in only one number cannot be part of it. Note that 24 and 36 actually share both their primes (2 and 3), so no unshared prime arises here — this error is clearest with a pair like 24 and 25, where 5 belongs only to 25 and cannot divide 24. The related slip for 24 and 36 is taking too many copies of a shared prime: use 2² (not 2³) in the HCF, because 36 has only two 2s.
If the overlap is empty (coprime numbers), the HCF is 1, not zero and not undefined.

Optional interactive version: dragging shared prime tiles into the overlap can recompute the HCF and LCM live, so changing which primes are shared updates both results. This is an illustration of the mechanism, not a required mechanism.
activities.rationale: Teaching HCF and LCM through prime factorisation and a Venn organiser connects the procedure to its meaning, instead of list-and-compare tricks, and directly targets the common HCF/LCM reversal. The Venn-to-HCF/LCM relationship is supported by the NCETM guidance; the CCSS claim supports that finding HCF/LCM of two numbers is a standard target.
sourceClaims: A Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors yields HCF (intersection) and LCM (union), making the relationship between factorisation and HCF/LCM explicit.
Grade 6 pupils find the greatest common factor and least common multiple of two numbers and use the distributive property with the GCF.
learnerActions: Write the prime factorisations of two numbers, e.g. 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3².
Place each number's prime factors (as individual copies) in a two-circle Venn diagram, putting the factor copies both numbers share in the overlap and the leftover copies in the outer regions.
Read the HCF as the product of the overlap (the shared primes, each taken at the lowest power both numbers have): 2² × 3 = 12.
Read the LCM as the product of the whole diagram (each prime at its highest power): 2³ × 3² = 72.
Check the relationship HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: 12 × 72 = 864 = 24 × 36.
Try a coprime pair such as 24 and 25 (24 = 2³ × 3, 25 = 5²): the overlap is empty, so HCF = 1 and LCM = 600.
activities.intendedInsight: A common factor can only be built from primes BOTH numbers have, taken at the lowest shared power — that is the HCF. The LCM must contain enough of every prime to be a multiple of both, so each prime appears at its highest power. The Venn regions are intended to make lowest-for-HCF / highest-for-LCM visible rather than a rule to memorise.

activities.title: Reference anchor: reveal the index form and the Venn result
feedback: Use any mismatch between prediction and reveal to pinpoint whether the slip is in factorising, in index notation, or in choosing powers for HCF vs LCM.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example is a useful anchor/reference for the format and the region logic. Its limit (noted in constraints): a fixed tree cannot itself be re-split, so it does not by itself demonstrate uniqueness — pair it with the build activity.
sourceClaims: A Venn diagram of two numbers' prime factors yields HCF (intersection) and LCM (union), making the relationship between factorisation and HCF/LCM explicit.
learnerActions: Study a completed factor tree for a number; before revealing, predict each leaf's prime value and the full index form.
Reveal the index form (e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5) and compare with your prediction.
Study a two-number Venn of prime factors; predict the HCF (overlap) and LCM (whole diagram) before revealing them.
Reveal the HCF and LCM and check your reasoning about which powers went where.
activities.intendedInsight: A worked tree plus Venn serves as a clear reference for the layout of index form and the intersection/union logic of HCF and LCM.

activities.title: Consolidation checks
feedback: For 360 = 2^□ × 3^□ × 5 the indices are 3 and 2 (2³ × 3² × 5); check by multiplying: 8 × 9 × 5 = 360.
Watch for an HCF/LCM swap: the smaller result (12) is the HCF of 24 and 36, the larger (72) is the LCM.
If 1 is placed with the primes, recall it is neither prime nor composite.
activities.rationale: Short checks consolidate results and can surface the HCF/LCM swap, but they test outcomes rather than build the decomposition or the uniqueness insight — best used after the build and Venn work. A sort checks classification but does not itself elicit construction of a factorisation.
learnerActions: Complete the missing indices: 360 = 2^□ × 3^□ × 5.
Find the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36 and state which is which.
Sort a set of numbers into prime vs composite (remembering 1 is neither).
Match each number to its correct prime factorisation.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of index form and correct HCF/LCM selection, with the prime/composite distinction secure.

activities.title: Socratic challenge: why is factorisation unique and why 1 isn't prime
feedback: If the learner says a different tree could give different primes, prompt them to actually build it both ways and compare the leaves.

If they can compute 12 but cannot say why the method works, connect it: because each number is ONE product of primes, their common divisors are exactly the products of shared primes, each used no more times than it appears in both numbers (including 1, using none) — so the HCF uses each shared prime at the lowest common power.
activities.rationale: A Socratic probe suits the conceptual core (uniqueness, why 1 isn't prime); dialogue can prompt justification but recognition of a correct statement does not by itself guarantee the learner can produce the reasoning. Best paired with the build-and-compare activity, since manipulation is what makes uniqueness concrete.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors/multiples, HCF, LCM, and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property.
learnerActions: Respond to the question: 'Could 360 have a different set of prime factors if we split it a different way?' — justify your answer.
Explain why 1 is not counted as a prime, and what would go wrong with uniqueness if we allowed it.
Explain in your own words why taking shared primes at the lowest power gives the HCF, referring to what a common factor must divide.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the reasoning — common divisors are built only from shared primes, and every number is exactly one product of primes — is intended to cement the conceptual objective, not just the recipe.

constraints: 1 is neither prime nor composite and never appears in a prime factorisation; primes are the multiplicative 'atoms'.
A factor tree is only finished when every leaf is prime — composite leaves (4, 6, 9, …) must be split further.
HCF takes the LOWEST power of each shared prime; LCM takes the HIGHEST power of each prime present. These are different selections and are easy to reverse — guard against the swap explicitly.

A common factor is built only from primes BOTH numbers share; a prime appearing in just one number cannot be part of it. Where two numbers share all their primes (e.g. 24 and 36), the only error to guard is taking too high a power, not an unshared prime.
HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers holds for a pair; use it as a check, not as a definition.

Reveal-on-tap worked trees/Venns are reference anchors: they show the format and region logic but cannot be re-split or re-grouped, so they do not by themselves demonstrate uniqueness — pair them with learner-built trees.
Consolidation checks test results (recognition/recall) and do not elicit independent construction of the decomposition or the uniqueness reasoning.

Index notation should be connected to prior powers/indices work, and HCF/LCM grounded in motivating problems (sharing into equal groups for HCF; repeating events and fraction denominators for LCM) so the concepts have purpose.

Optional live/drag interactions (dragging shared prime tiles into a Venn overlap, auto-collecting leaves into index form) are helpful illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms, and their effectiveness relative to static anchors is not established.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims carry verified:false in the original row; treat the DfE KS3, CCSS 6.NS.4 and NCETM Venn-guidance citations as unconfirmed.

The KS3 source claim attached to the build and Socratic activities supports the curriculum content/convention (unique factorisation and product notation are taught), not the efficacy of the particular method; method efficacy remains an untested proposal.

Correction applied this pass: the unshared-prime feedback for 24 and 36 previously claimed their 'extra' factors of 2 and 3 'cannot divide the other number', which is false (2 divides 36, 3 divides 24). 24 and 36 share both primes, so the unshared-prime error is now illustrated with 24 and 25, and the 24/36 slip is described accurately as excess copies of a shared prime.
Self-audit arithmetic checks: 24 = 2³×3, 36 = 2²×3²; HCF = 2²×3 = 12, LCM = 2³×3² = 72; 12×72 = 864 = 24×36. Coprime example: 24 & 25 give HCF 1, LCM 600. 360 = 2³×3²×5 = 8×9×5 = 360. All consistent.
The original's catalogue framing that '3D adds nothing' for these abstract ideas was a product fit judgement; it is omitted rather than restated as a universal pedagogical claim.

The 'different tree, same primes' uniqueness claim is mathematically sound (fundamental theorem of arithmetic) and is retained as a demonstrable activity; its instructional efficacy as implemented remains an untested proposal.
The classic error of taking highest powers for the HCF (giving 72) appears only as a misconception to correct to 12, never as a valid option in a learner task.

probeDeeper: Why do you take the LOWEST power of each shared prime for the HCF, but the highest for the LCM?
Why can a common factor of 24 and 36 only be built from primes they both have?
Every number has exactly one prime factorisation — why does that matter for this method?
What if it had been 24 and 25 — what's their HCF, and what does the prime factorisation tell you?
assess.correctAnswer: 24 = 2³ × 3, 36 = 2² × 3²; the HCF takes the lowest power of each shared prime: 2² × 3 = 12. A child reasoning well explains that any common divisor can only be built from primes both numbers share, and taking the most of each shared prime that BOTH have gives the largest such divisor — resting on unique factorisation.

errorPatterns.pattern: confuses HCF and LCM — takes the HIGHEST power of each prime (2³×3² = 72) for the HCF
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason about meaning: a COMMON factor must divide BOTH, so it can use only the powers BOTH have (the lowest); highest powers give the smallest common MULTIPLE instead.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer of 72 for the HCF; child uses highest powers

errorPatterns.pattern: multiplies ALL primes appearing in either number, ignoring which are shared
errorPatterns.nextMove: highlight only primes present in BOTH factorisations contribute to a common factor; cross out unshared primes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child includes a prime that only one number has

errorPatterns.pattern: gets 12 by listing factors but cannot justify the prime-factor method — no link to unique factorisation
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the calculation; connect it to uniqueness — every number is ONE product of primes, so common divisors are exactly the shared-prime products.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct answer, but 'why does taking shared primes work?' draws a blank

errorPatterns.pattern: prime factorisation itself incomplete — stops before fully breaking to primes (e.g. leaves 4 or 9)
errorPatterns.nextMove: keep splitting until every leaf is prime; 4 = 2×2, 9 = 3×3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: factor tree left with composite leaves

responseLevels.gap: confuses HCF with LCM (takes highest powers), includes unshared primes, or cannot factorise to primes.
responseLevels.full: factorises to primes, takes the lowest power of each shared prime for HCF (highest for LCM), and justifies the method via common divisors being built only from shared primes and unique factorisation.
responseLevels.partial: computes the HCF correctly via prime factors but cannot explain why shared-primes-at-lowest-power works, or is shaky on the HCF/LCM distinction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Find the highest common factor (HCF) of 24 and 36 using prime factorisation. Show your prime factors, then explain WHY taking the shared prime factors gives the HCF — why must that be the biggest number dividing both?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Students can get 12 by listing factors without understanding WHY the prime-factor method works. The reason tier tests whether they connect HCF to shared prime factors and the uniqueness of factorisation — the conceptual objective — rather than executing a memorised recipe. The classic error (taking highest powers, giving the LCM) also surfaces.
